Blouses seem only to become more popular witi each ensuing season, and many of us are nosv rejoicing in those which we purchased when th< summer sales were in their first youth. It is a great mistake to wait till the last few weeks of tilt sales, as by that time things have got tumbled about and crushed and soiled till they have lost hall their value, and are really not even worth the startling reductions" price with which they are ticketed. Earlier, however, there is no such safe and certain purchase as a well-made blouse. Among the prettiest styles this season are the silk shirts for morning or travelling wear, with small tuckings down the front divided by a narrow box pleat, which boasts of a couple of rows of fiat gold, enamel or mother o' pearl buttons. The sleeves of such a blouse should not be of a very pronounced fashionable vogue, but, preferably, small bishop's sleeve set into a narrow band or cuff. Indeed, although there are many very fanciful sleeves to be seen, I always caution all those who want a considerable amount of wear out of their clothes, to avoid anything which is very marked in dress, as these fashions are 'as fleeting as they are popular. Already the demise of the loose sleeve which falls in a bell shape or a deep hanging pouf from the elbow to the wrist, is to be felt by those who can read the signs of the times, and therefore a moderate bishop sleeve will always be sufficiently up-to-date to satisfy the requirements of most people. let or hinaance some rrve aid' feet into the narrow rocky bed in which the torrent seethes and roars. Thus the fertile oasis girt about by the houses of Cima, is cut off from the grim mountain opposite, whose rugged face, all scarred by land- slips and avalanches torn from it by the storms and snows of winter, rears itself menacingly. About half way down the precipice a slender bridge spans the chasm; to it a zigzag path has been practised in and out among the crags and shoulders, taking advantage of every ledge and projection; and on the other side, carved out of the living rock, another path wanders upwards till it is lost in the protecting mantle of the dark pine forest. Up this pathway early one morning four young people gaily climbed, stopping now and then to gaze down into the abyss below, from which some- times a slender handrail, sometimes nothing at all, defended them. A wierd and terrible defile it was through which the roaring waters forced their way tumultuously, flinging themselves in impotent rage against the unyielding masses which , were, indeed the foundations and roots of the mighty mountains overhead. All at once they passed from the naked wilderness of stone and angry waters into the green shelter of the forest. Here the narrow footway wound between mossy boulders and drooping ferns, a trickling stream now bubbled gently between overhanging branches, and waving creepers anon lay in dark pools margined by cool damp mosses and star-like flowers. Overhead the slender pine branches interlaced, and the straight stems made aisles and avenues of nature's pillars. Yet onward and upward they climbed, until at last the forest opened out, the trees fell back and stood aside, and a clearing of bright green sward like a fairy's carpet, jewelled with flowers' purple and white, yellow, blue and red spread before them. Rows of tasselled larches swept round, and, casting long shadows, gently outlined without confining the limits of the clearing. Up overhead a dark band of green pines and then a huge peak, soaring valiantly right lip into the clear blue sky. Here the lithe party sank down amid the fragrant herbage, and gave themselves up to the joy of being alive. . After a befitting period for rest and contempla- tion, the vulgar needs of the body began to be felt, baskets and knapsacks were unpacked, and their contents spread out upon the grass. Catherine gathered a great posy of purple salvia and feathery meadow-sweet and laid it in the midst. Harry Coverdale looked round him:

"This dear perfection' is almost terrifying in its completeness. I asked myself a minute ago whether, perhaps, this might not be a wonderful dream, from which I should awake with only a keener sense of the imperfection of realities." "Poor human nature! How little happiness fills its cup!" moralised Antony. "But why suppose it full ?" asked Catherine. "There is one happiness for to-day, another for to-morrow ; each one is perfect in its way." "To-day is the apotheosis of our happy summer.. Something tells me a turning-point has come." It was Isobel who spoke; she sat a few yards away from the others, her back against the trunk of a larch, and a; large leaf full of Alpine straw- berries in her lap. "My holiday has nearly spent itself," said Harry. "How easily and swiftly the days have sped away!" "I want to go to the top of that ridge beyond us," said Catherine. "They say you can see up the valley into Austria. Shall we go?" "I am quite content with what I see from here," said Isobel. "This tender green and the blame and patches of purple and yellow and white and the 'grave decorative lines of the larches. I want to go no further. div.head: PRETTY BLOUSE.
div.p: A PRETTY BLOUSE.

white crystalline blouses with deep ecru insertions and yokes of grass lawn or Irish guipure, for these look well with any colour of skirt. White and coloured batiste shirts are considered very smart wear, some of these being prettily embroidered by hand. The very latest style, however, of batiste bodices is shown in the pretty blouse sketched. It is of plain white batiste as fine as muslin but less transparent. It is made with inch-wide tucks, one overlapping the other, in the front and centre of the back, with small stiff cuffs upon a moderately full sleeve. A snrah or satin cravat is passed beneath the guipure lace collar. This is the smartest blouse imagin- able, but must be made of a batiste of a fine quality and be well cut. Such a shirt blouse would do well for seaside wear with any linen skirt, white, blue, pink or cream, and a worked leather or silk band. There is a new belt just introduced for we with linen toilettes. This is made of a coarse filet lace bordered with narrow bands of white or coloured suede, and fastened with small buckles and tabs. These are certainly very pretty and smart, fitting the figure to perfection, besides being cool and light, but they have one rather serious drawback, and that is that, being trans- parent, they fail to hide completely the junction of bodice and skirt. Shaped satin ribbon belts finished down the centre back, by a row of small buttons, and in front with an ornamental buckle, are very modish and becoming, as are also those of blurred Chine ribbon of a floral design.
The smart yet useful dress depicted is made of a soft grey twilled woollen material and the

div.head: 'USEFUL GOWN.
div.p: A 'USEFUL GOWN.

simple coat bodice can be worn corer a blouse or with a front of lace and muslin. The skirt is simple and of a convenient walking length, while the coat can be worn open to show the blouse or front beneath, or buttoned up in double breasted fashion. For travelling or for wear on one of the dull days we meet with so often now, atere is nothing so convenient as a dress of this kind, which is at once soft and warm and yet by no means heavy. Woollen materials of different sorts are indeed very fashionable this summer, as womankind has found out that they crush and soil less easily than muslin, and are really so light in texture that they are almost, if not quite as cool as the more diaphanous fabrics.

Ribbons are much in evidence this season for trimming purposes, and there are some very lovely floral designs. The hat sketched is trimmed with one of these dainty ribbons. The shape is of the flat low-crowned description, so much in vogue. I recently saw a very picturesque hat worn by a charming young girl. It was of burnt straw, and the trimming consisted of a small wreath of foliage round the crown, while one of the latest complexion veils was loosely draped across ,the face and caugh just by the tip of the chin. There is a tendency to curtail the length of the fashionable veils, which sometimes are arranged to come only to the line of the month. to be either very simple or very elaborate-.--therE is no medium. The more dressy varieties are trimmed with black and white ostrich feather:. while the plainer styles are of soft straw bent into becoming curves to suit the face of the wearer, with the brim bordered with an inch of black velvet. All the hats show a tendency to lie low upon the hair at the back, with either lace or velvet ends depending. Burnt straw, as it is termed, is the most popular colour at present, and a black velvet bow or band is necessary to lts sUCCeM,
COQUETTE.

The Panama hat has had a short lived popularity, as it is now quite discarded by the best class of people. No one will weep over its departure* as there are very few, even amongst the most smartly dressed women, who can wear a Panama hat to advantage, and when the multitude took to wearing cheap imitations nothing could save it from well-merited obloquy. Men too are giving it up, and taking once more to the smarter, neater and infinitely more becoming straw hat. Colours likely to be much employed by leading dress- makers this autumn are petunia, violet, Crates and green, the russet shades too, which are so attractive in tweeds and bomespuns. wi,l not be omitted from the list. Very simple in outline and detail are the newest walking costumes, pipings and strappinge of velvet, suede, or plain cloth, being all the trimming the tailor Permits himself. In the torn-down collar, and cravat however, there is a wide field for individuality. Plaids are being utilised for both purposes, and very smart is the effect they give. To look as though she had been welted and poured into her bodice was at ere time the great aim and object of the well-dressed woman. Nowadays, with the exception of the riding coat, we prefer the suggestion I rather than the sharp defining of the shape. This sounds and looks more easy,but it is nothing of the kind. The lining must fit 'faultlessly, and in the apparently easy draping of the fakes over this, great skill is [required. Leading modistes are turning out all thei• 1" dressy blouses and bodices elaborately draped and trimmed and moreover fastening at the haak, or in the most complicated manner at the side. To those amsng us who possess a maid, tie idea matters not at all, but to the woman who has to dress and undress herself it is I a worry' and should therefore be avoided.

Little coats of every kind and description are being worn, and among the more nqeful varietiea IR that of dark blue cloth, emartly strapped and stitched, and adorned with gold buttons. which can he worn so succes,fully over a white gown. These little coats cover the hips' are tightly fitting behind, and loose in front, and are built of divers materials, and in every colour. During the past two seasons we have greatly missed this useful.i. general "kind of coverioe.and with the autumn rapidly advancing we (Mall fled it s great bPrn again.

Isobel opened the door and walked out and he followed. When they were in the open air, walk- ing towards the gorge; she said : "Take care lest you waste your time. Are you ' sure there is anything to reveal? I may be a hollow sham. A thing of tricks and whims and below them nothing." "That, too, would he worth discovering" said Antony imperturbable. "How many feminine souls have you dissected, put under your microscope and added to your collection? ' "Hundreds, I should think.N "And you have found them all worth the trouble?" "Everyone. Even when awo nan is in herself of little value, a small thing, a poor specimen of her sex, even then, taking her place in the great mosaic, fitting in and filling up a corner or a back- ground, she has her value." "A patchwork quilt would be a better simile. A thing of bits of scraps laboriously put together and not worth the trouble it has cost when it iE done." Isobel spoke almost sharply, losing her usual level tone with its slight drawl in irritation at Antony's coolness. She was vividly personal and intensely individual in all her appreciations, and she felt the self-control on which she prided herself breaking down, under the galling suspicior that she was merely being made an object of study. Yet, the situation had an unexplicable attractior for her. They had reached the level of the bed of the torrent by this time; a great precipice sprang ur beyond it and nodded forward over the chasrr through which the water swirled and surged. "Look at those reckless idiots," she cried, point. jog upwards, and there above their heads on E jutting crag sat Catherine and Harry Coverdale perched up like gulls on a rock high over the roars log torrent; they seemed unconscious of all tin world save one another. "Never mind them. They will have the luck which always attends the foolhardy. Come, an sit in this sunny little corner under the shelter o this rock, on these log. beseems a sane persot with a respect for her fife. Here ! I brought thi; rug to make a comfortable seat for you let mo roll the end of it into a soft rest for your back; pu. your feet on the thin end. N ow, is that right?' Isobel had a cat-like love of comfort, and like( to have her natural wants deftly ministered to, ant she forgave Antony much as she slipped nimblj into the place he prepared for her and let him tuck the corner of the rug round her feet. The sight they had come to see was characteristic and sufficiently interesting. Between the rocky walls of its bed the torrent bears hundreds of thousands of logs,-the spoils of many a noble forest I from the high slopes of the surrounding mountains I to the plains below, and as they are borne tumul- tuously down, at Certain points, where projecting crags or huge fallen boulders obstruct the river's flow, they get jammed across and form a huge dam ever growing as more and more logs are piled against it by the rushing waters. Companies of omen, skilled in the dangercus work, descend into the bed of the torrent. Standing on the firmest of the logs or on the wet and slippery boulders, they strive with long poles, ending in iron hooks, to dislodge and dispatch downwards the heaped up masses of logs. When these begin to stir and yield, the men leap backwards, sometimes only just escaping before their foot-hold sway, and gives and goes thumping and plunging down the boiling current. The roaring of the water, the shouts of the men, the hollow crash of the moving masses of logs all add to the exciting tumult of the scene, and when the main body of some great pile has been upheaved, and one after another a score of smaller blocks follow in quick succession with a sound like rolling thunder, and the men spring back and scramble for their lives, the spectators are thrilled by the prevailing emotion and join in the general shout of exultation. I Presently Catherine and Harry Coveraale scram- bled down from their point of observation and joined the others. "Isn't this splendid?" said Catherine. "How he village girls must admire these brave, active fellows I'
"You are a born hero worshipper, Miss Wood," said Antony. "What a pity you did not live in the days of knights errant 1"
CHAPTER 111.

At the meeting place of three valleys the dividing mountains fall back, and a cup-like hollow, lined with green maize which shivers and changes as the wind passes over it, fills the space between the encircling walls of the upspringing mountain sides. Along a ridge around this verdant cup the houses of Cima cling, their wide over-hanging eaves and carved timber balconies breaking the sweeping line of the curving ledge, until just where perches the little white-washed church, the ground suddenly breaks away and a precipice_plupgea down without

But Coverdale was already en his feet offering his hand to Catherine as she rose from the grass; they walked away side by side, brushing aside the starry blossoms and the bowing grasses as they moved among them. "What splendid energy there is is in both those two !" said Antony, looking after them. "I suppose Coverdale needs it all to support him in the dismal life he has chosen. What will Miss Wood expend hers upon ?" "They are both full of hope. For them there is always something finer beyond the ridge. Is that the secret of happiness, or is it its dirge?" "I can never settle that point to my satisfac- tion," said Antony. "It is a question of temperament," said Isobel. "How do you bear it ? ' asked Antony, after a " What ?"

"Life in a hospital ward." "I accept what I cannot avoid. I wished to be a doctor, but my father opposed my studying medicine, so I was forced to take up what is called the womanly side of the healing profession. That is to say, the one which involves the greatest amount of drudging with the smallest possible recompense." "The gullibility of your sex is stupendous," said Antony, smiling affably. "I have given up inter- esting myself in what are called women's questions, though all my sympathies are naturally that way. I cannot stand the worry of trying to help people who will not help themselves." "How can most of us help ourselves? The spoke is put in the wheel of our lives too early. How can I recover the time during which mykther kept me idling about at ' home? He refused the necessary money for my studies, money which was granted without a thought to my brothers. The result is that they are rising Professional men, and I—a nurse on £2B a year." For the first time since he had known her Isobel spoke out her thoughts, as they came to her, gazing straight before her, careless what effect her words pro- duced.

"It is not too late, study now." "Where is the money to come from?" "Is that all?" " All ! It is eVerything." "How strange I" said Antony, musing. "To let such a paltry obstacle thwart your whole life's desires and ambition. My experiences have been yours reversed. My father gave me a first-rate education r then he ordered me to make use of it tc earn money. I saw the uselessness of it—l have no business capacity—my father was rich, and my tastes and capacities lay in directions where money is not made. I refused to be forced into uncongenial labour which I kneiv would be abortive, and in the end I gained my freedom." "But your father did not absolutely refuse you the money to live on in your own way? " Yes, he did." Isobel made an impatient gesture. "You borrowed, I suppose. That is what a woman cannot do." "I found a sympathetic friend who understood my position, and having more than enough wealth to satisfy both our needs, had the nobility of soul to offer to enable me to live the life which alone could be fruitful to a temperament like mine. I allowed no ridiculous pride to frustrate so simple and natural an arrangement." " Well,'l found no such friend," said Isobel, shortly. "You have such a one—now. Here/' said Antony, looking at her very earnestly out of hii wide-open blue eyes. "Don't suggest impossibilities. Your friend was af your own sex." A curious expression crossed Antony's face. "No ; she is a woman." Isobel sprang to her feet. "There they come, it is time we started home again. Catherine, what a long time you have been. Help me to put these knives and glasses tilt° the basket. We shall be late for dinner." Catherine looked surprised at Isobel's unwonted fussiness. "And if we are late for dinner?" she lueried. But seeing her friend was really anxious to start, the helped to clear up the relics of the lunch, and uhey started down the path through the pines. Isobel slipped her arm through Catherine's, and they walked on first together, leaving the men to follow; all the way back this order was adhered to, ,)ccept when the path grew wide enough for them so walk abreast. There was not much conver- sation, a lassitude seemed to hang over them all; -,he morning's joyous verve had subsided, and a wearied re-action set in. When they came in sight of the door of the Buon' Ei inico, they saw a carriage standing in front of it; the occupants had evidently entered the inn, but >everal tall boxes were in the act of being un- oaded. "New arrivals !" "And swell ones." "Tol" grand to come by the posta !" "They have driven wer from Bordone, I suppose." These were the -emarks that rose to the lips of one after another is they walked up to the door. When they came plite close, Antony exclaimed, "'Why, those are Pheo's boxes, she must have arrived." And starting forward, he ran indoors. The others .00ked at the labels on the boxes. ' "Mrs. Haig," they read out, in tones expressive

Many men who have made their way in life have been big eaters. Premier Seddon, and Pierpoint Morgan are names which immediately occur to the mind ; while it is a well-known fact that the great Napoleon died from a:disease brought on by eating too freely of his favourite dish—stewed onions. Eating means, or should mean the intaking of energy. While this was the case with Napoleon, he was great. When his digestion gave out, he became weak, ill, and at last succumbed. Every worker, men or woman, should know that the appetite is the index to the health. Can you eat? Can you store up energy ? If not, you should not work and expend it, Is your digestion sound ? If not, look to it. If it is weak and disordered, it is a screw loose in the great machine which continues your existence, and if it once becomes lost, it can never be replaced. For tunately, nature has provided a remedy for all digestive ailments. Chas. Forde'e Bile Beans when taken, assume in the body the extrt form of nature's own bile, and aid digestion, clear the bowels of accumulated impuri- ties:and fermenting food, and stimulate the liver in the only well, which nature has said this shall be don. Don't take mineral medicines, but take nature's own vegetable cures. Nature makes your ailments,let nature cure them. Bile Beans being purely vegetabls are nature's own remedy. div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The King is understood to favour the revival of dress carriages for guests invited to attend the Court. Such I an equipage is very different from the ordinary landau or brougham, being more like a State coach painted in the family colours, and it has a gaudy hammercloth, covering the coachman's box. During the early years of Queen Victoria's reign such carriages were always used by the nobility on State occasions, but alter the death of Prince Consort, they became the exception rather than the rule. The ordinary and less showy vehicles came into personal use, but the King objects to the same carriage as is used in the mornings for shop- ping purposes being driven up to Buckingham Palace for Court entertainments, and it ie not unlikely that the full dress carriage may come into vogue again. This would naturally delight the carriage builders, as the least expensive of these gorgeous equipages cost not less than £5OO or £6OO. Though the King is very liberal in extending privi- leges to the public it is very difficult to obtain permission to view the royal gardens at Windser. The first thing one observes is, that the crown and royal initials are on almost everything. Carts, wherslbarrows, flowerpots, implements, and machines, all are branded, and though a new set ef moulds is now in ure,mos; of the tools have the letters V.R. upon them. Nearly all the fruits and vegetables that adorn the Royal table are obtained from the Progmore gardens, which have now been enlarged to about sixty acres. Over two miles of walls are devoted to wall fruit, and the glass houses cover an immense space. Every variety of fruit is grown, and a special feature at Frogmore is the cultivation of pineapples. Needless to say they are the very best that can be pro- duced, and the pineapple the medical authorities tell us, is an excellent aid to digestion when taken with after dinner dessert. The shootings in most parts of the country have been unfavourably affected by the bad weather during the spring and summer. That is a matter, however, which concerns only the rich and well to do, but the general holiday season has also suffered from the same cause. The complaints of the hotel and lodging-house keeper at the seaside,and in the country have been plentiful, as visitors were seam, and the sufferers generally apportion the blame between the weather, the Corona- tion, the war and the taxes, and the general increased cost of living. Certain it is that those, who looked for- ward to the Coronation year as one of exceptional prosperity, have been grievously disappointed, but the real reascn why holiday resorts are not doing well this year arises from the general increase of household ex- penses. Owing to increased prices, the general experi- ence of the housewife is, that it costs a fifth or a sixth more to keep up the home than it did three or four years ago and consequently families have so much less to spend on holidays. Charles Dickers advised anybody who had a grudge against an insurance company. to buy from it an annuity, and then go to live at Yarmouth, where the bracing air of the East coast would enable him to live to an aye which would bring the company to the verge of despair. Another opportunity for a similarly good inveatment seems to have arisen in the slime county here Mrs Rix, of the Pop3's Head, Norwich, has cele- brated her 100th birthday. The mother of Mr,. Rix was 104, and she has a sister-in-law in the neiehbouring county who ;s also 104. If there are any ,more of this long-lived family an insurance company would no doubt be pleased to assure their lives, but it is doubtful whether an application for an annuity would be received with equal enthusiasm. Women.are sometimes spoken ef as the difficult sex, ano it must be admitted that they are more prone to petty quarrels and jealousies than are men.. This is the main reason why no attempt leas hitherto been made to start a Rowton House for women, on similar lines to the high-class lodgin,e-houses which Lord Rowton has been instrumental in ?minding for men. The Rowton House is sometimes called the poor man's hotel, and it is ear% tainly a great success in providing the working classes with every comfort and decency at a minimum cest.The difficulty in providing similar institutiors for the other sex has arisen ,from the fear that a mixed colony of women would never get'on well together, and that a few quarrelsome spirits would always be upsetting the general haipsony. The experiment is, however, at last to be tried3ndif it proves a success it will go far to solve the problem of how to provide for the working girl and the "bachelor woman" in the great industrial towns.

A QUESTION OF TEMPERAMENT
BY MARY L CAMERON.
PART IL —CHAPTER 11. (continued.)

The next day Antony Haig and Mr. Coverdale went for a long walk together; they returned about half-past four, at which our hour Isobel and Catherine were in the habit of making tea, to the wonder and amusement of the simple-minded host and hostess who had not yet leamed that hot water could be charged for in the bill. Antony was always invited to share this little feast, and Mr. Coverdale was now included in the invitation. Catherine made the tea, , boiling the water on a spirit lamp at a table in a corner of the sala, and when it was ready Antony came and fetched cups for himself and Isobel. Harry Coverdale was standing at the window, half on the balcony, with his back to the room looking out; he seemed to have forgotten about the tea. Catherine looked round; Isobel and Antony had their heads together over some photographs, and were too absorbed in them and each other to notice anything else; she took a cup of tea in one hand and a plate of biscuits in the other and walked over to the window;. Coverdale did not stir, so she touched his elbow lightly with the plate. He woke suddenly out of his abstraction and turning, found the gracious cup-bearer close to him, with the round white wrists and throat and the long lines of her soft creamy white dress falling round her. A quick flush mounted to his temples: _ _—

"A thousand pardons! I am ashamed of myself. To be waited on by you I " "Don't you think you want to be waited on a little ? " said Catherine, and her eyes rested on his kind tired eyes with a diffident gentleness that was almost a caress.

Coverdale took the cup, rather doubting if he were awake, so strange it seemed that he should be served by a beautiful girl. The days sped by and the little party welded itself together. No more visitors arrived; Cima remained still undiscovered by the tourist crowd. "Where is Catherine?" asked Isobel, coming into the sala one morning and finding Antony Haig its only occupant. "I thought we were all going down to the gorge to see the lu floated down after the rain." "I have not spoken to Miss Wood this morning,' mid Antony, looking up from a note book in which ae jotted down under the heading "Isolated im- pressions " a variety of rather jerky sentences embodying his passing mood and ideas. He had a projected volume of essays floating in his brain and hese were to form its nucleus or backbone. "But," tie continued, " Coverdale told me he was going on to the gorge half an hour ago." Isobel walked to the door. With her hand on bhe latch she half turned her head:

,"Shall we join them, Mr. Haig ? " Antony jumped up and walked towards her. "I did not offer to go with you, because, to tell the truth I thought that you kept apart from me the last few days and feared I had done or said something tactless or presuming for which you wished to punish me." Isobel smiled, looking on the floor a little to one aide of Antony's feet, he moved nearer to her. " Did I ?" she said. . .

"I thought so, and it depressed me." Antony's voice was pleading, almost tender, but Isobel still Looked aside and he saw the long lashes against the clear olive of her cheek and felt he could almost have sacrificed the best pages of "Isolated Impressions" for one of the strange quick glances, he had begun to watch for. "And I thought that perhaps the analysis was complete aad that no further studies from the life were needed," she said. And under the heavy lids a glance shot straight into Antony's wide open blue eyes. Some men would have lost countvance and been at Isobel's mercy for ever after. , Not so Antony Haig; he received the shot as a feather bed receives a bullet, without a shock ; he smiled a patient smile. "How little you know yourself, Miss Knight Years of research would still leave something un- revealed." _ _
)1` surprfse an ISewlfeti
landlord eame
mt.
'The signora has arrived," he said. "What signora? Who is she?" asked riatherine.

"Why, the wife of Signor Haig, I suppose," said the landlord, looking puzzled. "Tony married 1 Impossible 1" cried Coverdale. Isobel walked straight into the house. Catherine followed more slowly with Harry. "It is very odd," she said. When he arrived he said he had to wait here for a friend, but we thought you were the friend." "No ; our meeting was quite accidental." "Mrs. Haig! He called her ' Theo,' " went on Catherine, wondering. "She must be his wife." "But why this mystery ? " said Harry. "Oh 1 Mr. Haig likes mysteries," replied Catherine, "he thinks them interesting." When they assembled in the sala for dinner, they found that Mrs. Haig had taken a private sitting- room, and Antony was dining in it with her. This seemed natural under the circumstances, and the three remaining ones made no further allusion to the absent. After dinner they separated. Harry went out to smoke and the girls to their room. Catherine leaned her arms on the window sill and looked out on the shadowy outlines of the moun- tains looming through the silvery darkness of the summer night. Behind one peak a faint disc of light, like the aureole round a saint's head in an old picture, tinged the sky with a solemniight ; it grew more and more intense till a line of silver outlined every curve and angle on the peak, then the glory centred in one point, and, escaping from the screening heights, the moon sailed forth into a cloudless sky. "How beautiful everything is! But—how puzzling !" "We make puzzles for ourselves and each other. Things would be simple enough, if people were honest and straightforward," answered Isobel. '" Do you think that is all that is wanted? Oh, I wish I could think so." _ _

- _ "Playing at hide and seek is very good fan for a time, but one must never forget that it is a game, and that the artfullest wins," Isobel went on, following out her own thoughts. "In a woman duplicity is called modesty, and straightforwardness, boldness; suppose one had the courage to fly in the face of tradition, and act as a man would under the same circumstances," said Catherine, also engrossed with her own problems. Isobel got up and came to the window. "What do you mean by acting as a man, Kitty?" she asked, putting her arm round her friend's waist. "It seems to me that a man acts just as it suits him where women are concerned. He has a code of honour in dealing with his own sex, but it gkows very elastic when he applies it to his deal- ings with women." "And we must always keep our real thoughts and feelings hidden in self-defence? What a cynical view of the relations of the sexes 1 I hope it is not true. Oh! Isobel, I do so hope it is not the true one." _ .

"Dear idealistic Kitty I I hope you may not find it so. There may be a few Sir Galahads still wandering about the world, let us hope you will find one. Only take care that you do not find out too late that your idol has feet of clay. Now let us go to bed. We only make things worse with thinking about them. When lam back in the hospital ward and you in the office, all these speculations will seem very much aside from the real business of life." (To be concluded.)

div.head: GIRL TYPIST'S SORROWS.
div.p: GIRL TYPIST'S SORROWS.

Among the occupations which women Fem better adapted to All than men is that of typewriting, the nerve-straining monotony of the work having less effect on the feminine constitution, But even young women do not escape the ill effects, as is apparent 'from the statement made by a prepossessing young lady employed as typist at Redditch, Miss Maude Niblotte, living at Holly House, Prospect Hill, Redditch, told the enquir- ing reporter :
TYPIST.

- When I was sixteen (that was four years ago) I began to suffer from ausernis. Now at twenty I am a healthy girl, for which I thank Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people. Previously I had never been very strong, and the assenia caused great exhaustion ; I was unable to do even a little work. I was so weak. Going upstairs I was forced to rest hAlfway oc account of shortness of breath. Then I had indigestion,and suffered acutely from pains between my shoulders and in the chest. My elan became yellow. I was attended by a doctor for some monlls,but I felt no better,l seemed to grow worse."

"And what led to your happy escape from this ? " asked the reporter. The reply was unhesitating : To nothing else but Dr. Williams' pink Pills for pale people. 1 rema.ined in that terribly weak state for several months, and then I hearl that a friend of mine bad been benefited by Dr. Williams' pink pills, and I determined to try them. I obtained a box and although I found no very marked banafit at first, after taling a second box I began to feel better. My appetite improved, the indigestion disappeared, and alter persevering with the 011 a I now feel better than I ever .did. Ido not think I should be alive now if I had not beard of Dr. Williams' pink pi 11,." _ _ _

Miss NibJetts added that she had recommended Dr. Williams' pink pills to many friends, all of whom had derived great benefit. div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Wycliffe PS. A. Society.

At a meeting of this society on Sunday, the chair was taken by Mr George Wallington, who based a brief address on the following words inscribed on a Cheshire homestead :—" Take thy calling thanktully ; love thy neighbour neighbourly ; shun the path of beggary." He advised his hearers to aim at having a really good character and they would find it was the happiest path. Mr Mellender, of Manchester delivered an address on "The greatest thing in the worl I," which he showed Was love. Miss F Farrar, of Halifax,very sweetly sang two solos entitled " The Beautiful City" and " The Star Of Bethlehem. The service was also taken part in by lir Owen and Mr Farrar. Choir Sermons at Hill Cliffe.

—..—. These special services took place on Sunday anal the 'weather unfortunately turned out to be most unpropi- tious. In the morning there were special hymns, and a aermon by the pastor Rev J S Hughes on "Musics in the Sanctuary "and in the afternoon, there was a service Of Song entitled " Primrose Garth " rendered by the Choir, under the leadership of Mr Percy Randall, M.I. C.M. the readings being given by the Rev J S Hughes. Solos were given by Miss Mlles and Mr George Moss and the whole service was of a pleasing Character . The rain however came down in drenching torrents, just at the time of service and militated against a good attendance. By the time of evening tier- 'vice the rain had subsided somewhat and there was a good attendance, when the sevice of song was repeated under the leadership of Mr George Moss, the pastor again giving the readingstand preaching a short sermon on " Music in the heart." Mr W Hellas acquitted him- self ably at the organ all day and in addition to accom- panying the various sacred songs, gave a number of voluntaries from the masters. The coll,ctions—which Were taken by members of the choir—amounted to 3 satisfactory sum. Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church.

Special services were conducted in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Leh-street on Sunday, by the Rev Gardbarn Rued, late of Glasgow,who has recently taken over the charge of this church. At both morning and services there was a good attendance. In the -dog Mr Reed took for his text a part of the Bth verse of Mark 14 "She bath done what she could,"which served for a foundation for an eloquent and inspiring discourse on Christian service. Contrasting Christ's verdict on the action of Mary the sister of Lan trus,who had arnointed His head with spikenard, with that of some.! the disciple; who were indignant at what they termed a waste of precious ointment, the preacher went on to say that true Christian service was spontane- ous, wholehearted and e.self-sacrincing and pointed out that in the 17th Century service in the church was nearly always proscribed an in consequence the moral life of the period was very low. In speaking of whole- hearted service the preacher earnestly pleaded that each One should ask himself if he could in all honesty say that" he had done what he could" adding that to . have such a eulogy passed by Christ upon life's conduct was more to be desired than the highest honours earth could bestow. Baptist Church Golborne-street. A large congregation assembled in rhe ahovo place of worship on Sunday morning when the pastor gave the fourth of a series of talks on " Christian Verities." The subject under discussion was the Christian conception Of God based on the words " God is Love." After a brief review of a previous lectern on the" existence of God "the preacher said, that to prove the existence of God was one thing but to prove the existence of a good God was another. They might he quite sure that there %fere evidences of a mind or an intelligence in the uni- verse but there existed much doubt as to whether that Intelligence was a good or an evil intelligence. That they should form right aad proper conceptions of God was very importaw, because the Conception they had of God would give colour to their life and conduct. Man had always refleoted in this life the idea be held conceraing 3od. A city or a State never rose higher than the religion of its people, tle had told them in a previous lecture that the purpose Of religion was to present God to man and that a religion was true in the degree in wh oh it gave a true idea of God. The preacher went on te say that there Were only three aggretsivo religions. All others were slowly but surely dying, and those three were : Buddhism, Mahommedanism and Chriitianity. Briefly but vividly the preacher portrayed God as pro- claimed by each of these diff rent teachers. According to Buddha God is an eternal process, a vague, impersonal indefinite umoncious law, which found its logical clevelopenent in the eadness 'which characterised all Buddhistic literature. The God of Mahommed is a " Being " vho is practi- cally" Fate " rather than an intel igeat Proviefeace. He aproclaimed God as a Being, one and spiritual, but whose spirituality is so harsh and cruel, that He can be dellghtd bv the massacre of Greeks and Armenians. The Ged proclaied gy Jesus is not only an Almighty Sovereign b3t a loving Father, His plans and purposes are all in tho intereets'ofLove p . FlthPrhrld was not a state of Deity but its centre. In concluding ,a discourse Over which lasted 410 minutes, the preacher said that ai Christ had taught that they need tokaow, and all that is their momsnt„r deepest longing tared to know concerning God. In etvheenei nve evening e theis tj,h,psi was well fined. Next Sunday a t o te a Baptismal service when the pastor will preach et:, Distinctive Principle of the Baptist Church." Will of Lord Gerard. Colonel William Cansfield, second Baron Gerard Of Garwood, Newton-le-Willows, Lancashire, and late of the 2nd Life Guards Of Castwell Park, Bent, a member of the jockey Club, who died on the 30th July last, aged fifty-one years, and whose estate has been valued at £142,519 13i 31 grots. including Personalty of the net value of £14661 3s 2d, appointed as executors of his will of the 29th Sep- tember, 1899, with a codicil of the 15th June, 1902, his brother-in-law, Sir Martin Is Merchant Hadsley Gosselin, of Blakesware, Herta, and Captain Frederic Gerard of Kinwaton House, Alcester ; and the testator bequeathed to his wife, Mary Emmeline Laura,daughter of Mr ienry Beilby William Milner, of West Retford House, £l,OOO and the income during her widowhood o' a sum of £30,000, which, subject to her interest, is left in trust for his younger children. Lord Gerard be- queathed to his valet, Charles Peacock, the income for life of a sum of £2,000, and he bequeathed the diamond necklace, stomacher, and pendants which he inherited from his father in trust to devolve With the barony, and to be for the use of the wife of the successor to the title. He left the effects at Garswood to his son Frederick Joh*, now third taron Gerard, and he left the residue ef his pro- Derty in trust for such uses as if it were money arising under the Settled Lands Acts from the sale of settled real estate. By this will the late Lord Gerard charged the settled estate with certain pay- Inents, which were revoked by the Codocil. There e no bequests to tie Roman Catholic Chunk.

THE RIGHTS OF RAILWAY
TRAVELLERS.
Interesting Particulars.

While the tolday seas; is here it may not be out of place to give our readers a few hints on talir rights as railway traveller/. They are based on the authority of a contributor to our excellent contemporary the " Globe." The railway companies make bye-laws, but if they are unreasonable,and even if they have been sanc- tioned by the Board of Trade, tee courts will not allow them to be enforced. Various rail way companies have tried to lay down the principle that a passenger who is found travelling without a ticket shall pay the fare from the place where the train started, but no law will have none of it. The passenger is entitled to say where he actually started from, and in default of the company being able to prove that he is not telling the truth,it can claim no more than the fare from that station. It is entitled to demand We name ani address—which,b7 the way, should never be refused—but unless there is good reason to suppose he i 9 giving a false one it will be open to an action for false imprisonment if it detains him while i verifie s it. DOS'S` PAL FOR LOST TICIIETS.

_ Many people think that they are wi'hout reme ly if they happen to hava lost their ticket. Bac the ticket is only the evidence of the cootract, not the contract itself, and whether the missing ticket be a single or a return half the simple erg-alien,: of furnishing the col- lector with one's name and address will avoid any neces- sity for paying the fare over scam. OF course, it is a serious offence to travel without having taken a ticket at all and then seek to evade payment by giving a falate name and address ; bat, speaking generally, all offences of this character depend upon the e cistAnce of an intent to defraud, and when there is no such intent—and it is for the company to prove there is—there can be no offence. It is the same in a case of a passenger who travels in a class superior to that to which his ticket entitles him. Ucless he does so with intent to defraud, the company can onfy claica from him the difference in the fares, and not that if there was not proper accom- modation in the class for which he took his ticket.

div.head: COMPANIES BOUND TO PROVIDE SEATS.
div.p: COMPANIES BOUND TO PROVIDE SEATS.

The company is bound to provide them with seats either in the class for which they have takei tickets or in one superior to it, and any damage which may be saffered, by delay or otherwise, through failure to do so will blrecoverable from the company. Wr is there any need for people to submit to overcrowding. When a compartment has as many passengers in it as there are seats, any occupant may resist an attempt to add to their number, and in doing so he is entitled to use so much force as is necessary for him to eff !et his object. A passenger who takes a ticket for one station and gets off at another which is short of it must be careful to ascertain that he is not travelling under specially cheap rates, or he may have to pay his fare over again The railway companies are very properly allowed to aid in developing particular resorts by the i9qUe nf cheap fares to them, and a passenger is no entitled to avail himself of these facilities to reach somewhere else which happens to be nearer to the place from which he started But if he has paid the statutory fare he may get out anywhere he pleases on the journey and his ticket will be good. The notice so frequently found on ordinary tickets that " if this ticket be used for any place but that named upon it, the full fare will be charged," is of no force, and if the traveller chooses to go beyond the station named upon his ticket, he will bo liable for nothing mere than the excess. The railway company is bound to deposit the passen- ger at the destination for which it has issued the ticket. and it must do this within a reasonable time compared with that which is advertised. If it fails to do so either through the failure of its own train to reach it or through inability to make some connecticn which it has undertaken to make, the aggrieved passenger is entitled to assist it to keep its contract by taking post-chaises and so forth and charging cost to the company.
MISTAKES IN CHANGE MUST BE RECTIFIED.

If the c-impany declines to sond him on by a special train it will have to pay for his board and lodging dur- ing the period of his delay, and will b 3 responsible for any damage he may have sustained in consequence of his detention, provided that huch damage is not too re- mote, and might reasonably be exoected to flow from it. But, of course, there must be moderation in this as in eve2ything else, and the gentleman who had no par- ticular business in Scarborough, but who insisted on being taken there by a special train rather than submit to a delay of an hour and a half, was very properly non- suited by the Court. Timid people are apt to think that because ther3 is a notice over same ticket-offices to the effect that no question will be entertained as to the correctness of change unless it be raised at once, they must put up with the loss, where they have paid half a sovereign in- stead of sixpence and have not discovered the mistake until they have got into the train. Singular as it may seem,railway companies are not entitled to set aside the Statute of Limitations in thia serene way, and if the passenger :um swear to his less the debt will be reccver- able from the oeseipotent company just as though it was an ordinary individual. It is a question of evidence and nothing else. The Courts have never been able to get nearer to a definition of passenger's luggage than that it is some- thing that the passenger will naturally require, either on his journey or at the end of it, and which is done up in a package. For instance, if a man is going on a sporting tour his guns and hie rods will be passenger's luggage, which, within the limits of weight.the company must carry free, but a bicycle and a bath-chair will not be so. To show how difficult it is to arrive at any rule upon the point it is sufficient to say that one pair of sheets has been held to come within the definition, while six pairs were ruled to be outside it. If a pas- senger has a through ticket and is delayed on the road he is entitled to require that his labelled luggage shall be placed in the cloak-room and no charge can be made for doing so. It is also worth mentioning that the com- pany's liability for the loss of luggage does not cease, as !Amoy imagine, because it has been put by their porter in the carriage with the passenger. It remains precisely the same as though the luggage had been placed in the van.

In any dispute with a railway company it is not a bad plan to lay the matter. in the flrat before the Board of Trade. There are many instances in which the instance, i department is bound by statute to mediate, and in any cage the aegrieved party will not prajudice his rights by making the application,

div.head: TELE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, AUGUST 22, 1902,
div.p: TELE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, AUGUST 22, 1902,

little army of his brother offieers in blue peremp- tory injunctions no: to suffer anyone to eater on any consideration whatever before morning. Whilst I was chatting with another member of the force in Little Dean's Yard, 133015 obviously important personage came up to anxiously enquire what arrangements had been male for the safety of the Regalia during the night. " Six Yeomen of the Guard are stationed inside the building, with in- structions to watch it in rotation, two by two," was the reply " Those old fellows are all right," said the important personage a trifle dubiously, " but is that sufficient ? " afterwards enquiring as to the exact location of the rich insignia of royalty, and its accessibility from the outside. The policeman told him that he was on duty at the entrance to the Yard, j that the only other dangerous point was on the other side the building, and that, there,another man was stationed; whilst, of course, all round the building further members of the force were keeping constant watch and ward. And then he did his bast to en umerate the crowns and sceptres, orbs, and rings, and swords, which had been carried up those ancient stairs,atal rested now within the dim old room. R was a tempting catalogue, imperfect as I knew it was, and I felt ' like some conspirator as I accidentally caught their conversation, and strolled furtively away ; bat I subsequently read that even the precautions which I have already mentioned aid not adequately repre- sent the care which had been taken to prevent mishap, and that the Abbey would be searched from end to end with lanterns ere the morning came. Outside I met Sir Frederick Bridge and Canon Welldon, genially conversing with some mutual friend, and,passing thence into the crowded streets, I sauatered by the great Canadian Arch—that tri- umph of imperial a lvertisement —into the Strand, and felt that I was justified in ordering dinner. At sunrise, as I lay in bed next morning, I was waken_d by the boaming of the guns,which ushered in the memorable day. I was knocked up at half- past six, and, at eight, was driving through a Chickening stream of fellow-citizens toward Trafal- gar-square. I passed amid the rapidly increasing Crowds, along the line of route, up beautiful Pall Mall and broad St James's-street (still lovely, if not quite so beautiful as in thegolden June),and stately Piccadilly, and cool Constitution Hill, towards the Palace gates. The sanded streets were lined at every point with smart policemen or well-seasoned troops,and everywhere already the side-walks were filling with an eager multitude, the windows and the stands alive, and everywhere broad flags, and fluttering streamers, mottoes, and festoons of rain• bow richness and variety lent colour to the unaccustomed an) heart-moving scene. As far as Hyde Park earner, I had stemmed an endless stream of carriages, from which provincial Mayors looked forth in gilded robes and chains,or pretty peeresses peeped shyly, or their coroneted husbands did their best to look at home, whilst soldiers, admirals, and foreign potentates, and wealth, and power. and fame, and fashion, rolle i in endless sequence towards the Abbey. Anon, I met with marching soldiers, mounted officers, or rousing mili- tary bands ; and soon, in Constitution Hill, I noticed, with a thrill of pride, on either side the specious ro ad, some fifty of our own " South Lance- shires " as brave a regiment as any in the realm. Directly opposite the Palace, whence the Royal flag was floating in the transitory sunshine, I perceived a mighty band of coffee-coloured warriors in whom I recognized at once our gallant Indian Troops. I had seen them in their camp at Hampton Court, had chatted with them at New Brighton Tower, and watched them picturesquely grouped upon the ferry boats at Latchford Locks, but I never saw them quite to such advantage as to-day. There they stood, with fiery steeds, and turbaned brows, and great dark eyes, and flashing lances, opposite the Palace of the King. At last they were " to see his face" indeed,and it was quite an inspiration to have placed them hers, and let them be the first to greet him as he sallied forth on his high errand on .." the mast important day' in all his life," But how few of them speak English. I tried quite half a dozen, wishing to im- press them with a sense of this distinction ; bat could only get vague words of thankfulness that he was better, and was really to be crowned at last. On down the leafy Mall I went, through double lines of brave be-medalled warriors, and here I met once more the representatives of our devoted kith and kin beyond the sea. The Anodes were amongst them, I observed (alone among the coloured races), and most soldier-like the members of the great colonial army looked beneath the spreading shelter of the ancient trees. Our own brave Volunteers were stationed here, although it was not till the journey home I learnt that I had passed immedi- ately in front of them, for, try one's best, one's eyes completely fail to take in all the splendid details of a scene like this. On by the mighty stands which flanked the Horse Guards, and beneath the gloomy arches leading to Whitehall; and here I found still greater crowds, and new excitements—cumbrous sand-carts lumbering slowly to and fro ;high officers continually upon the mov e ; long lines of half familiar faces—swarthy Malays, yellow- skinned Chinese, the sturdy Ghoorkas, the wild sons of Borneo, fierce eyed West Africans, the coal-black troops from the West Indies, and se- dately marching to their places with bare feet and door-mat heads of hair, the gallant children of Fiji. My object was, if possible, to get right opposite the entrance to the Abbey, but I turned aside a moment to observe the passage of the peers and peeresses along the wooden gangway leading from the House of Lords. In straggling groups they sauntered slowly by, a curious glimpse of coronets and purple robes, or daintier coronets above bare arms and shoulders ; and I wondered whether to be most amused or most impressed by the unwonted spectacle. But one of the particularly favoured few allowed to witness it who stood beside me was not in much doubt upon the subject. "Upon my word," he said to a companion, laughing heartily, " this is about the funniest thing I've seen. It's just like ' lolanthe '1 " The mighty stands around St. Margaret's, the Hospital, and the Aquarium were already full, the roofs and windows occupied,and heads were visible in distant windows half way down Victoria Street. Directly opposite the stately annexe to the Abbey, with its tiny statues of the seven Edwards and its wonderful fidelity to ancient detail, I took up my post. Huge wooden barriers shut off the public on the northern side. The Abbey doors were guarded by the Beefeaters,in red and gold, and by long lines of helmeted police. Across the approaches to Dean's Yard a little body of Chinese troops were drawn, and there they stood with curiously impas- sive faces all the morning. The path in front of us was kept by a great double row of Irish Guards, with their huge hairy helmets ; and, beyond them, to the .right. Were stalwart Bluejackets, who took their places to a rousing cheer, and towering English Guardsmen, and brave " British 'Grenadiers." The flag flew gaily from the square tower of St Margaret's ; beyond, we caught the stately outlines of the Houses of Parliament, and, high upon the balcony above the Abbey's Western door,a grave policeman who stood there alone until the solemn rites were over. The damsels at the Deanery,and at the great hotel directly to the right of it looked out from roofs and upper windows in excited groups ; a multitude of straining eyes I gazed down from the twin towers of the Aquarium 1 and, though everybody was supposed by this to be I already seated, coroneted peers and peeresses drove up from time to time in carriages which frequently suggested all the splendours of the Lord Mayor's Show. Within the doors of the annexe, we got a fleeting glimpse, at inter- vals, of famous figures, and the Duke of 1 Devonshire,in coronet and robes,stood calmly taking in the scene for several minutes, whilst, upon the other side, we saw the master of the stately rites. the brave, black-bearded, sallow, short, but truly noble, Duke of Norfolk, Earl Marshal, and heredi- tary head of the nobility of England. From far away there came the murmur of the mighty multi- tudes which reached in an unbroken circle all along the line of route, A young "Sphere" artist stood I beside me, solemnly deputed to portray "Dick " Seddon, who, he had been told, was coming to the Abbey with a special guard of honour, Whether 1 Mr Seddon brought his guard of honour or not I cannot say, but, though my friend was on the qzti vine all the morning, certainly he did not pass our way. The Premiere, I fancy, must have entered by some other door,for,though we both watched eagerly we did not catch a glimpse of them, whilst such of the devoted Commoners of England as could spare a day from the wild moors had passed into their places through the southern transept. In front of us was Mr Melton Prior, the renowned war artist, evidently very much at home, and every moment some distinguished personage passed by, or some great officer rode proudly to and fro and presently a stirring cheer arose,and,whilst we craned our necks to learn the cause of it, up drove a royal carriage, with the young Prince Eddy and his brothers, at ithe windows,thePrince,a sun-locked child I greatly like, with boyish zest, saluting his delighted future subjects very gravely as he glided slowly past them to Dean's Yard. A scarlet group of royal footmen

div.head: LIFTING OF THE
div.p: THE LIFTING OF THE
CLOUD.
Impressions of the
Coronation.
[By ARTHUR BENNETT.]

The cloud upon the capital had gradually lifted when, the day but one before the Coronation, I drove through its familiar streets once more. Bat the sobering influence of the calamity of June was visible on every hand in August. One missed the golden sunshine, and the decorations, though in many places lavish and effective, were not half so general or on so grand a scale as those which made the leading thoroughfares a dream of loveliness six weeks before. A multitude of stands had dis- appeared, and it was only when you reached the actual route of th 6 proce:?sion that you felt the imminence of same unique event. Upon the afternoon preceding Coronation Day I drove through deepening lines of well-dressed people waiting in the rain in Regent Street to see the Q leen upon her way to take the chair at the great annual meeting of the Soldiers and Sailors Families' Association at Q.men's Hall. I reached the entrance in good time, saw presently a tiny escort, and the gleam of scarlet liveries, and,seated in the Royal carriage, with Princess Victoria and the Duchess of Argyll, the Sovereign Lady of these realms ; and, standing on the steps within the portico, alone, I saw her sweet face at the window, humbly raised ray hat, and was rewarded by a special bow all to myself. How beautiful" the See- king's daughter" looked, and how astonishingly young ; and, as I watched her during the brief pause before the carriage drove round to th 3 rear, I did not wonder taat her people worshipped her. Inside the spacious hall, well filled with a distin- guished audience,some grass blunderhead had raised a temporary platform high above the ordinary stage and fenced it off from everybady with a towering 1 wall of flowers. I watched the royal party enter- ing, to a tremendous cheer, and saw Her Majesty politely bowing her response to the ovation, and acknowledging the loyal greetings of the brilliant company assembled on the platform ; but, as the music of the National Anthem died away, and she sank gracefully into the chair, she might as well have vanished like a pantomime fairy through some magical trap door far all I thenceforth saw of her until the meeting closed, although I had a splendid seat almost in the front row, right in the body of the hall. No wonder that the " Daily Telegraph " sent forth a growl, next day, at the absurdity of building up between the people and their Queen that" absolute barrier " " of pink ivy— leaved geraniums, lilies, spirma, hydrangeas, and marguerites, set amid palms and smilax 1" It also practically hid such interesting oriental potentates as the Maharajas of G /Jailor and Babbili, the Nawab Fetch All Khan, Sir Jamsetjee, Jeejoebhoy and Lady Jeajeabhoy, and brave Sir Pertab Singh ; and such distinguished ladies as the Countess Roberts, Lady Audrey Buller, and Lady Methuen, net Sc' mention quite a crowd of generals, admirals, and well-known noblemen; and the builder must have been extremely proud of the success which had attended his ingenious eff arts ta conceal them from our vulgar view. .__ . .

In my provincial ignorance, I half expected that the Queen would act like less exalted chairwomen. and take the conduct of the meeting in her own fair hands. But everything was done by deputy. 'The Queen commands me," said suave Colonel Gildea, the chairman of the Association, " to read the report." And a very interesting report it was. On million three hundred thousand pounds had passed into the Association's hands since the com- mencement of the War; well-nigh four hundred; thousand wives and children had received its aid and Mr Lucas Tooth, a rich Australian who had given the King ten thousand pounds toward the London hospitals, had given the Queen Gen thou- sand more for its especial use. The "Queen commanded " Colonel Glide°, next, to ask Lord Grenfell—of Egyptian fame—to move the adoption of this singularly pregnant docu- ment, and bluff old Admiral Freemantle, to second it; and, after that, to ask General Cameron to move, and Rear-Admiral Hughes-Hallett to second the re-election of the Council. Both resolutions were adopted, almost silently; and then—Lord Roberts being absent at the Palace by the King's' command—the Earl of Northbrook rose to move the usual if unusually important) vote of thanks, alluding warmly to the King's touching message to his people published in the press that day; and adding that nothing could have better shown the interest taken by the Queen in the Association than that, at this time, and under these circumstances, she should have graciously presided over such a meeting. Sir Edmund Barton being also summoned to the Palace by the King,Sir Albert Hicae,the Prime Minister of Natal,was asked to second the proposal. Sir Albert, a most estimable gentleman with a kindly face and heavy white moustache, declared that it was the greatest honout of his life, and, in his pardonable wish to rise to the occasion, he gallantly said that her Majesty's image was en- shrined in the hearts of her subjects, at least three times; hut he evidently meant it all, and I liked I him. The vote was carried with immense enthu- siasm, but acknowledged simply by a kindly bow. However,it was quite enough. Queen Alexandra's look was eloquent, her presence better than the best oration; and when somebody commenced "God save the Queen " (or King)—l was not very clear upon the subject—we all sprang up and sang it with a fervour which was not to be restrained. And then Her Majesty shook hands with the distin- guished folks about her—being very gracious to Sir Albert—and through the windows of the corridor I watched her slowly drive away. " Did you see the Queen?" I heard a female Londoner inquiring of a lady friend outside. " Yes, did'nt she look lovely ? ' was the response. To which the first retorted,some- what acidly, "She looks younger than her daughters There isn't one of them her equal in any way!" I strolled back past the Palace, where "a small in, vestiture," it seemed, had taken place—this was the reason why Lord Roberts and Sir Edmund had been absent from Queen's Hall—to that not less import- ant Palace by the Thames, which was about to close its mighty portals for a two months' holiday ; but the flag on the Victoria Tower was lowered before I reached it, and I Was only just in time to see the last of the poor jaded "Members" leaving Palace Yard. The Peers, however,were still sitting. They were discussing trout fishing, a cynical policeman said. It was a subject in which they all were interested, and they would probably not ad- journ for another hour or two. And so I went inside, and was lucky enough to find ,Lord Newton, who conducted me into "the Gilded Chamber" where a dozen noble lords or so, the Duke of Devonshire, as Leader of the House, among the number, were assembled, like a family party, around the dumpy little Lord Chan- cellor. I heard some nobleman I did not recognize express his pleasure that the Bill had passed. I saw the Duke of Devonshire get up to say that the House would adjourn for a couple of months, at which Lord Halsbury mumbled something which I could not catch ; and then the last of our heredi- tary legislators also went to their well-earned repose, or peradventure to try on their coronets against the great event next day. Upon the occa- sion of my previous visit, the great hall of West- minster had been arrayed as a huge dining-room for the convenience of the Members who intended to be present at the crowning of the King ; but the hall was empty now, and many of the Members were, understood, so tired that they could not ev en wait to see the Coronation !

Proceeding to the Abbey, and passing through Dean's Yard, I came upon a glittering royal carri- age and an army of policemen ; and, soon.a band of deans and canons and the like emerged from the approaches to the Cloisters, bowing low to two distinguished-looking persons asithey enttqed ic;: hen four red-liveried lackeys—whose legs,to me, looked somewhat artificial—mounted theirprecarious places and the dazzling equipage drove silently away. At first I wondered if the rumour that the King would come, that day, in person to inspect the Abbey had been actually realized. It was not even a prince, I found; but none the less the visit was distinctly interesting, for the royal carriage had borne hither the Regalia from the Tower, and this had been conveyed, with reverent solemnity and pious care, up those old steps in that sequestered yard which led to the Jerusalem Chem-' bar, and here the priceless treasures were to rest until the hour of the great rite arrived. I sauntered round the gray old Cloisters, noticing the specially erected wooden stairs and entrances which led to various portions of the Abbey by convenient, if unfamiliar, ways, observing in one corner the im- pressive legend, " The King's Box and the Royal Household," and politely asking a particularly affable policeman if he could not possibly let me have a peep inside. "I should stand a chance of being beheaded if I did," he laughingly replied. Re- turning, I heard Canon Hensley Henson giving to a

occupied the pavement where I stood, and one of them replied to something I was bold enough to ask about the Queen by calling her •' a dear lady," and describing several actions he had personally witnessed of such thoughtful kindness as to make one quickly understand his lo‘e Long as the time of waiting was, it swiftly slipped away, and shortly after ten, a body of Guards approached, with jingle of accoutrements and flash of steel, and, almost ere we realized it, we were gazing at the first procession. Eight Royal carriages in turn drew up immediately in front of us ; the steps were lowered, the doors flung open, and we saw the occupants dismounting one by one, and disappearing in the shadowy portals of the venerable church. The Duke of Cambridge, very old and feeble, got out slowly from the first of them, and naturally received a royal wel- come ; whilst the Princess Beatrice, the Duchess of Connaught, Princess Louise, and the Duchess of Albany, together with the younger members of their various families, were keenly scrutinized and warmly welcomed, as were, indeed the representatives of all the other Royal Houses, and amongst t Jena, specially Prince George of Greece, the Duke of Sparta, the Crown Prince of Deumark,and the enterprizing individual known to everybody as Prince Fleury of Prussia A. closing escor7, of the Horse Guards; then another eager interval, then more Horse Guards, and then the second procession, which consisted of two car- riages containing such mysterious personalities as chamberlains and women of the bed chamber ; and then, eccompanied by yet more Horse Guards, and to yet another cheer, the Prince of Wale and hie sweet consort, still best known to most of us as Princess May. The Prince is growing bald, but looked extremely wall ; and everybody must have felt the special fitness of their presence at this great imperial celebration, recollecting that protracted journey round the world which they had lately made to draw the links of &moire clo•er, and to bind all portions of the King's dominion; to the Mother Country and the ancient Uhroue.

Meantime, our ears were thrilled by the dull booming of the great guns at the Tower and in the Park, and instinctively we looked each other in the face and said " The King has started ! " With keen expectancy we waited, almost silently; and, as we waited,l could picture the resplendent retinue proceeding through the Palace gates, end slowly moving down the Mall, amid the double lines of valiant warrior., and the loval millions whom they restrained ; and, even as I pictured it, we heard the sound of cheers, which fliwed in front of them, and swept like some great tide into our quiet corner as the first instalment of the third and last precession suddenly came into view, More Horse Guards; then in wondrous garb, the King's Bargemaster and tvvelva:mystic Watermen; and then four carriages; which bore "the Household of their Majesties" and then a dazzling group of Aides-de-camp to the Commander and the Prince of Wales, includ.ng half a dozen Indian Princes; and, upon their heels, the Aides-de-camp to the King, eight representing our devoted Volunteers,and seven our gallant Yeomanry and nine our bold Militia: and, then three Indian Maharajas, still more dazzling in their robes, and gems and gold ; and, then, no less than eighteen representatives of the Regular Forces, including Hamilton and Plumer, , and ten distinguised naval officers, amongst them Commodore Lambton, whose great naval guns saved Ladysmith ; and then, to a tremendous cheer, Sir Alfrea Gaselee, and Admiral Seymour, and the plain, straight, capable, strong, stern, warm-hearted, statesman-like and blue-eyed Kitchener ! With the exception of the King he got the test reception of the day, and who shall say that he did not deserve it ? After, these in swift, succession, came the Headquarters Staff, some thirty-four in all, all notable and chief amongst them Kelly-Kenny and the ever popular old apple. faced, white-haired, victorious, and resourceful little " Bobs."

Behind this splendid company of soldiers followed five and twenty Yeomen of the Guard,tie picturesque as usual; and then a group of equerries including several princes; and then to ringing cheers a splendid escort of Colonial and Indian Cavalry, and still more Horse Guards, and, then, to such a wel- come as I never beard the King receive before, a coach that almost dazzled one, with its sigh cream-coloured horses,and its four majestic golden figures, and its great glass windows topped with tiny crowns; and, then, the ever young and ever lovely Queen—the darling of her people—and, a I trifle pale. I thought,l and thinner than when I had seen him leave the train at Paddington sit weeks before, His Majesty the King ! I never saw him looking quite so kingly, and my heart went out to him with a new loyalty as suddenly the State' Coach paused. the steps were lowered, a cluster of great figures gathered around the door, the fair face at the window disappeared, and we saw the twain dismounting quietly ; and then,amid a hushed and reverent silence, watched them pass- ing on into a vista of such power, and fame, and splendour as had never met in all the annals ot our race before. Behind him rode his royal brother, and the Royal Standard'followed—though, in my desire to see the King, I did not notice it with Major General Trotter, and a crowd of Dukes, and Silver Sticks, and other courtly folk ; and finally the Royal Grooms and the inevitable Life Guards once again, and then the Abbey doors were closed, the dull boom of the guns was heard, once more and the event to which for:months the Empire had been looking forward had commenced at last. ( To be concluded.)

Tuesday was the last occasion on which the public bad an opportunity of access through Westminster Abbey to view the arrangements for the Coronation and 18,650 persons oassed the turnstiles. Altogether during the seven days 96,907 people have been admitted, and the receipts amounted to £4929. This amount Is to be applied to charitable purposes. A WATERSPOUT IN SCOTLAND.—Dtiring the heavy rain- storm on Monday what appeared to be a waterspout was observed at Sakti Railway Station. A huge column was seen gyrating across the meadow to the south of the Dubbin It travelled with great speed across the stream to a field on the farm of Knowes, where it levelled eighteen ricks of hay to the ground, and then subsided. The water in its progress made a great swishing noise, and caused astonishment amongst those who saw the phenomenon.

div.head: CORONATION
div.p: THE CORONATION

ffot since the great Naval Review held in honour of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee has such a superb and imposing array of ships of war assembled in home waters as that which was reviewed by his Majesty on Saturday and Monday. It was indeeda fitting finale to the series of memor- able and magnificent pageants which have con- stituted the Coronation programme. Of the historic events of the past fortnight only one has had more interest and a deeper significance for Englishmen, and that was the solemn ceremony in Westminster Abbey when Edward VII. was crowned King of all the Britons. The Spithead display was perhaps the most wonderful manifesta- tion of sea power the world has ever seen. No other country—indeed, no two countries—could assemble such a fleet under like conditions. It was no picked gathering of warships, but merely the concentration of vessels nearest to hand—the Channel Squadron, the Home Squadron, and the Cruiser Squadron, together with the torpedo-boat flotillas of the home ports and some ships com- missioned for special purposes, such as the training ships, alone formed the long and stately lines between which the Victoria and Albert ploughed her triumphal way on Saturday, and which steamed past the King's yacht as she lay at her moorings on Monday. Not a single vessel had been summoned from abroad, and not one had been put in commission to add splendour to the spectacle. It was a grand and impressive scene—one which will live forever in the memory of those who witnessed it. Admiral Sir Charles Hotham has good reason to be a proud man to-day, for the supreme command of such a fleet on such an occasion is surely one of the highest honours of the Service. The Review on Saturday was a glorious success, but the brilliant spectacle prepared for the evening was consider- ably marred by the terrific storm which broke along the South coast, rendering the illuminations almost invisible from the shore.

Unfortunately the evolutions of the fleet planned for Monday, ,which, under favourable conditions, would have eclipsed in point of interest ~ithe stationary exhibition of Saturday, had to be practically abandoned owing to the wretched weather. This was a great pity. for no ,such spectacle has ever been seen since the general introduction of steam into the Navy. The famous gridiron move- ment is frequently practised at sea, but in English waters no such display has ever been held, and, of course, never has a Royal yacht with the Sovereign aboard been the object around which the somewhat intricate manoluvres have seen
MONDAY'S NAVAL SPECTACLE:
THE WAP.SITIPS STEAMING PAST THE kING.B YACHT.

executed. As it was, the fleet merely filed past the Victoria and Albert in two lines, manning ship but not saluting. The two columns after standing for some miles straight southward, bent their course somewhat westerly to sea and subsequently dis- persed. However, to see the great ships of war steaming majestically past the graceful yacht was, in the King's own words, a "magnificent sight." Very little of the stately pageant could be seen from the shore, and the disappointed spectators ashore who braved the elements to catch an occasional glimpse of it can only hope for better luck next time. The Shah of Persia has met with a right royal reception in this country, and his Majesty will or certainly ought to return to ht own land with a very high opinion of English hospitality. On his arrival at Dover, on Sunday, he was welcomed in the name of the King by Prince Arthur of Connaught and on Monday the
