and visits to the Empire and the Hippodtonte are amongst other diversions of the week, so that his Majesty can hardly find that time hangs heavily on his hands, especially as he has the reputation of being an acute observer. This is the first time the present Shah has visited England, but it is con- fidently expected that he will follow his father's example and come again. Lord Miler's recent visit to Delagoa Bay is s point of very great interest in the settlement of South African affairs, and it is hoped that it will be fraught with considerable consequences. Delagos Bay, in a word, is the key of the Transvaal and must play a large part in the promised development of this important new Colony, as by the Portuguese port and the connecting railway, Johannesburg is Fo much more accessible not only for emigrants, but also for the necessary imports. In fact, the value of Delagoa Bay cannot be overrated, a fact which in the past has not been sufficiently realised, as twice we might have become possessed of it, and on both occasions let the chance slip. Short, after it was awarded to Portugal by Mars MacMahon's decision we could have bought it, b did not. Again, in 1879, Mr. Morier (afterw art,.

div.head: DELLGOA BAT
div.p: DELLGOA BAT

WHICH SEEMS LIKELY TO COME 'UNDER BRITISH CONTROL. Sir Robert Morier), our Minister at Lisbon, ob- tained for us the concession of immunity from dues and charges of all kinds on imports to the Trans- vaal yid Lorenzo Marques, and the definite right to use it in time of war for the embarkation and disembarkation of troops, munitions of war and stores, for the purpose of forwarding them thence over the frontier. This would recently have saved us an incalculable amount of cost and trouble, but Lord Beaconsfield did not realise the importance of it, while it clashed with Mr. Gladstone's Majuba policy. Last December. however, we arranged a modus vireai, and it seems that Lord Miler's visit will result in a far more satisfactory state of affairs. Hitherto the whole of the Portuguese administration has been hopelessly inefficient and grossly corrupt. In customs, harbour, railway, and everything else, bribery and self-interest of the officials have played the largebt part. The harbour, naturally one of the finest in the world, has been made as inadequate as it possibly could be, while the docks and railway accommo- dation have been out of all proportion to the demand. The sanitation of the town has made it a death-trap, and the whole place has been almost impossible for Europeans Now, as a step to regeneration and possibly to ultimate purchase, it seems likely that we shall build a new harbour and adequate docks, and in return take over the control of the customs and railway as a guarantee of repayment—a step which will be of great mutual benefit alike to Great Britain and Portugal„, as our interests are identical with respect to the TransvaaL Lord Miler's visit, although an- nounced to be merely personal and complimentary, was anticipated on all hands with the liveliest interest, and it is indeed good news that it has been "most satisfactory.?' The reorganisation of this essentially unsatisfactory spot could not be in better or more capable hands.
The morbid curiosity which hitherto has invari- ably attracted a sensation-loving crown to the A a gaol on the morning of an execution e•-s_ns
THE BLACK FLA& WHICH WILL PLX. sze r.orn, ON THE MORNING or AX EXECUTION.

will no longer be gratified by a sight of the familiar emblem of a shameful death. The Black Flag has been abolished, and now the publia will have to be content with the usual formai announcement in the Press that a crime has been expiated and that the executioner has done his grim work as humanely as possible. Few will regret the disappearance of the dismal signal—the last relic of the days of publis executions, when it was thought that the sight of the scaffold was a more or less effective warning to would-be murderers. One wonders that the Black Flag was not done away with when the Private Executions Act came into force, as served no useful purpose, but only pandered to the depraved hankering after the gruesome whick posseages some people. div.p: This is just the reverse ot the French piece of in- tolerance, but it is quite as galling and quite as unjust. And the same consequences will follow. We, too, have our Brittany. Wales is quite as tenacious, quite as courageous, and quite as religious as the old Celtic province of France. he Carnarvonshire County Council, for example,

as already made up its mind what to do. It will simply ignore the Education Bill, refuse to levy rates, and decline to take over the work of the School Boards. Probably, other Welsh counties will follow suit, and perhaps some English towns where Nonconformists are strong and the School Board pop-dar. In that case what will Mr. BALFOUR do ? He will behave, no doubt,as he did in Ireland. He will resort to coercion. The police will be called in—perhaps even the troops which were used at Pearhyn may be requisitioned again. And when the County Council has been dealt with it will still be necessary to" sell up" with every accompani- ment of violence the thousands of Nonconformists all over the country who will refuse to pay an unjust rate. A spectacle of that sort will be no more popular in England than it is in France. No Government could survive it. This Bill can only be passed by the votes (1) of the Irish members, and (2) of the eighty Unionists who have privately protested against it, though they did not dare to vote against it. But even the Irish members object to Clause 7, and they will certainly not support a policy of coercion. As for the Unionist Nonconformists, their position will be quite impossible. The Government would collapse nuserably before such a resistance as this.

Tun Tory party, of The Right to course, simply refuses to Resist. believe that anything of the sort can really happen. Imagination is not the strong point of the average Conservative, and Mr. BALFOUR, the author of "Defence or Pnilo- sophic Doubt,"is by temperament unable to under- stand 'enthusiasm. As some one said of Lord SALISBURY, he is only a bigot by calculation. But laith and enthusiasm are none the less realities. It only requires a real grievance of this kind to evoke them. We are a desperately respectable nation, nursed and lapped in convention, with a supersti- tious reverence for th 3 law. But that is merely because the law is on the whole decidedly just. Tyranny is a new experience, but it woald transform the natural character amazingly. And resistance would be abso- lutely proper. Mr. BALFOUR has no mandate whatever for his policy. The Education Bdlwas simply never mentioned at the General Election. After Bury, Leeds, and Belfast, not to speak of Sevenoaks and the o:kneys, Mr. BALFOUR must know perfectly well that the country is against him. Unless we are to wait tamely for four or five years until another General Election comes round in the normal course of things there is no remedy open but this of direct defiance. This however, it is necessary to add: No one desires to force the conflict to extremes. Such a struggle as this would be bad for education. It would redouble sectarian bitterness, and it would lower the nation's dignity. The way to avoid it, how- ever, is to make clear beforehand, by petitions, by public meetings, by covenants to refuse to pay this rate, that we really are in earnest. Then, perhaps, Mr. BALFOUR will yield in time.

Those who are thinleng of embarking for South Africa in search of employment would do well to 1,. wait a little longer. A correspondent in Cape Town, writing on July 30th, assures us that over five-sixths of British South Africa,martial law still prevails and one cannot move even from town to town without permits. In some cases it has taken four or five weeks to get a permit for a special town. Intending emigrants will therefore see the difficulties which beset thorn at the present time. Whatever chances they think they have, will not be much injured by a delay of six months. Prices are frightfully high and all 'the towns intensely congested.A rush of emigrants will only aggravate • matters and those who are wise will wait until the conditions are more favourable.
l I I

The doings of the three railway companies which compete for the traffic between London and the North may soon become a legitimate topic for public curiosity. Apparently they have been none too prosperous of late, and since " trusts " and "combines" are in the air they have discovered that it is competition which reduced their divi- dends, and already they are talking about the possibility of amalgamating in some more or less intimate union. The corupetition,one may observe is really none too strenuous. Not one of them has been stimulated to provide an express service as rapid as the North of France Rill way gives without the stimulus of any competition at all,and their goods rates are higher than in any other civilized country in tl e world. If such a system -flourishes at present,what suould we have to toler- ate if the stress of rivalry were withdrawn No doubt competition involves a great waste. The best routes are often missed,and fortunes are spent in needless advertising. But if there is to be a monopoly it would be intolerable that it should rest in the hands of a private company. The inevitable consequence of an amalgamation would be State control.

---- The reception of the Boer leaders by the King after the great Naval Review is one of the most , agreeable incidents connected with the Corona- tion. Generals :Botha, De Wet, and Delarey have received every mark not only of official but also of popular esteem. If more has not been done tbat is only because delicacy forbade it,since after all these brave men are still burdened with a great bereave m—the loss of the cause to which they had devoted their lives The bitterness of the s past three year has ;anished, leaving hardly a trace behind it. dN ot many months ago Mr. Chamberlain w "Standard"ouncig these men as "bandits." Theand the "Daily Telegraph "openly advocated th e shooting in nas cold blood of such of their men as from time to time. Mrs. D Wetewe captured was a defiant prisoner in a Concentration Camp. No calumny was too gross f(ar belief. Thethre generals whose hands the King Was grasping the other day were outlaws sentenced to banishment for life. All this is happily forgotten to-day, but I wise men will ponder over it. It is fashionable to talk of war as an experience which exalts a nation, and calls out all that is chivalrous in its soul. Is ' that really the fact ? In the heat of battle, no doubt, the soldier rises to moments of self-sacrifice and high daring. But what of the nation at home? It was not till peace came and we could think quietly that anything like sympathy or chivalry or generosity made its appearance. Then, to be sure, ia a moment we dropped the old angry atti- tude as though it had been no more than a con- scious insincerity. But while it lasted it debased and degraded and decivilised. War is not a moral tonic; it is a temporary return to savagery and to all the passions oc the savage.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
HONOUR FOR A RUNCORN VOLONTWER.

Local Volunteers will be pleased to learn that among those honourably mentioned by Lord Kitchener for their services in South Africa is Trooper Frederic T A11en,29918 of the 21st Company 2nd Battalion Cheshire Imperial Yeomanry. Allen is a native of Runcorn. Before he went to South Africa he was a member of the 2nd V B South Lancashire Regiment He has received a special communication direct from Lord Kitchener, and it is understood that some mark of distinction will be conferred upon him for heroic conduct in the field DEATH OF MR. G. Goner, RUNCORN.

The death took place rather suddenly at his resi- dence in Balfour-street on Sunday morniog, of Mr George Gorst, who during a long life was associ- ated with the business ot the town. A self-made man, he established himself in business as a grocer, and for a number of years was most succes,ful. He retired about ten years ago,the business being taken over by Mr Afellor,and lived for some time at Picow Farm, in the Holloway. lie was of a most genial and kindly disposition,and was held in the highest esteem. His wife predeceased him four or five years ago. The funeral of the deceased gentleman took place at the Cemetery on Wednesday. STARVING A. FAMILY AT WIDNES.

On Thursaay at the Widnes Petty Sessions, Kate Glassy and William Glassy, of Moss Bank, were charged with neglecting their two children. Mr Knowles, for the N.S.P C.C., stated that the eldest child, five years ot age,was in very poor healtb,and the youngest child was likely to die unless some- thing was done for it. The woman's two sisters would tell the bench that through the man's system of starvation the woman was almost of weak in- tellect. When the officer went to the house he bought some bread and the woman was so hungry that she ate it ravenously. Mrs Gleave, sister of the woman Glassy, said she was almost out of her mind through ill-treatment. She would feel satis- fied if the bench sent her and her children to the workhouse,—lnspector Hod ben and Police-con- stable Rutter said the house was in a shocking con- dition, and the children were verminous. The charge against the woman was with lra wn,and the male prisoner was sent to goal tor three months with hard labour. FUNERAL OF A RUNCORN BAKER.

On Wednesday afternoon the mortal remains of Mr Richard Richardson, of Bridgewater-street, were committed to the. grave at Runcorn Cemetery. He bad succumbed on Friday last to an attack of pneu- monia. He was 54 years of age- For 28 years he had been employed as a baker by the Runcorn Co. operative Society, and for many years past had been foreman at the bakehouse at the Central Stores. He was a member of the Duke's Club and the Amalgamated Society of Bakers, in which be took a deep and active interest. He was an enthu- siastic bawler of considerable skill. He was held in the highest respect in the circle in whin!' he moved, and the Committee ot the Runcorn Co-opera- tive Society, in a letter of condolence to his widow state that the Society has lost a good and faithful servant. Beside the mourners, his funeral was attended by about 100 people representing various societies, and including a large number of the employes of the Co operative Society- The Rev W Scholes conducted the burial service, Many beauti- ful wreaths were placed on the grave.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
BY A BORRESPONDENTn

At the pres'ent moment the eyes of 'all enthusiasts are turned towards the RuncDra football list. In a fortnight the football season will have commenced in dead earnest. A glance at the list shows tnat Runcorn will have some doughty opponents to meet ere cricket asserts its peaceful sway again. Nevertheless it is believed by nose "in the know " that the Linnets have rosy chances of securing the honours they prize so highly. Unfortunately, it is stated, :that Butterworth, who was expected this season to figure in the rear division, pat his knee out at one of the practice matches. This is a most regrettable incident, for it was believed by all that Butterworth's knee had quite recovered its former strength. In the other departments of the team there will be but little alteration, and with luck, Runcorn should come out, to use a well-worn phrase, " on top."

The" stores " annual trip to Morecambe, which took place on Monday, was a very enjoyable outing and a large number of co-operators took advantage of the special facilities offered to have a day's en- joyment. The weather was all that could be de- sired, anti all the arrangements were perfectly carried out by Messrs J :Shaw (secretary), and T Clare.

The wave of excitement which is sweeping over England in consequence of the Nonconformist op- position to the Education Bill has hardly affected Runcorn. Liberals will note that Dr Clifford and the other prominent Free Church leaders are act- ively engaged in thwarting the iniquitous measure which is being rammed down the throats of Britishers by tactics which savour of medieval days. There can, of course,be little doubt but that the measure will pass. The Government, domin- ated by clerical wirepullers, dare, not, in the last. lar,with iraw their hand from the ritualistic plough But it is when the measure is placed on the statute book that the real opposition will be felt. The much sneered at Nonconformist con- science will unquestionably make itself felt. Mean- while local Nonconformists are wondering what attitude the Runcorn Free Church Council will adopt. If they ar3 guided by the London Free Courch Council they will unhesitatingly recom- mend all local Nonconformists to band together and defy the tax collector. Whether loyalty to principle would bear such a strain is a debateable question, but there can be no doubt but that this is the simplest solution of the diffizulty, There may be exciting times in Runcorn yet, ere long.

Four years ago Mr S Taylor instituted a new manner of municipal entertainment. He made a departure from the dull, dreary, monotonous grind of garden partieß,receptions,at homes and banquets. In 1898 he took the members to Buxton tor a delightful day's enjoyment. Mr Wiswall followed his lead a year later when he took the members a ' sail up the Ship Canal to Manchester and down the Bridgewater Canal, a new experience for most of those concerned. On Wednesday Mr Taylor repeatPd his experiment with the happiest results. Hvery- thing that forethought and generosity could pro- vide was available and breezy bonny Derbyshire was seen under the best conditions. Some of the leaders of Runcorn public life also had the oppor- tunity of seeing how excellently Runcorn's most able and honoured citizen comported himself as a captain of industry. It is a character in which few Runcornians knew him.

div.head: ST HELENS TRADERS' AGITATION.
div.p: ST HELENS TRADERS' AGITATION.
The Outlook for the Small Dealers.

The " Times," under the heading " The passing of the Grocer," publishes the following from a corres- pondent The struggle which is now taking place at St Helens between the retail tradesmen and the cc-operators deserves more than passing notice, as it is an indication of what is proceeding beneath the surface all over the country with the exception of the South of England where the ce-eperative movement has never gained a serious footaold. Although all traders feel the co- aoerative competition to a greater or less extent, it is the grocery trade which feels it most keenly—first, because it is toe trade most seriously attacked ; secondly, because the trade itself is engaged in the internecine strife known as " cutting " ; and lastly, because it is threatened by other mortal enemies, the " comp any " shops, such as the some and Colonial Stores, the International Tea Company, Lipton's, et hoc genus octane. The individual or "single-shop " grocer, as his fellow-traders term him, is indeed between the, upper and the nether millstone ; and the process of attrition is proceeding at such a rate that in many dis- tricts he will soon have almost disappeared. During the last fifty years the conditions of the trade have undergone a complete change, which has converted the old-fashioned grocer, who required to know many things about the" art and mystery" of his trade, into a vendor of packet goods, so that a large proportion of the grocer's work of the present day could be accom- plished almost equally well by an automatic machine delivering a packet of goods in exchange for a coin. The disappearance of the "art and mystery" enabled out- siders and half-fledged assistants to set up as masters, and the increased competition led to a war of prices which has proved, and is proving, disastrous to the single-shop trader. Worse still, the eimpticity of the trade made the way easy for the co-operative societies and for the joint-stock grocery companies. The co- operative movement for retail distribution of goods has advanced by giant strides, the aggregate business of the co-operators —mostly retail—having increased from 15 millions sterling in 1874 to over 68 millions in 1699 ac- cording to the latest Board of Trade report. At the present time it is considerably more. Leeds alone,with I a population of 367,000 has a ea-operative society wi.h a central store and over 80 branches doing a grocery trade of £1,000,000 a year. Bolton, with a population of 115,000, has a society which shows yearly grocery sales of /shout £500,000. Manchester and Sal- ford have co-operative societies which do between them a grocery trade of over £600,000 year. When it is con- sidered that there are altogether about 1,500 retail societies, almost all flourishing and rapidly increasing I their grocery trade, it will be obvious to what a parlous state the ordinary grocer most be reduced in the , districts where co-operation flourishes. On the other hand, the company shops are pressing the grocer almost equally hard. These shoo are nearly all conducted upon the same iron routine system with automatic mansgers and still more automatic assistants, the brains being supplied from headquarter:. with the consign- ments of goods, every shop belonging to a particular company being a duplicate of every other sloop. There is no pretence of any " art and mystery" about this. One of these com- panies, and that not the largest, has over 250 branches ; and there are about half a dozen of these companies having their headquarters in Loudon, with many others in the provinces each possessing from ten to sixty branches. DAS year just past has been one of almost unbroken disaster for the ordinary grocer ; yet if we take a recent report of one of these companies, we find that it is paying a dividend of 15 per cent on the ordinary shares, and that last year has been the most prosperous the company has ever had. Ia the grocery trade at large the failures were the largest in amount ever recorded, and the trade easily headed the list with 934 failures for an aggregate amount of over £750,009.

div.head: FOOTBALL IN EARLESTOWN AND
div.p: FOOTBALL IN EARLESTOWN AND
NEWTON. Prospects of the Local Clubs.

Earlestown will commence the coming football season with better prospects than they have done for some years. The chief reason for this is that as a result of their splendid play last season. they are enabled to start with a balance of nearly £5O in hand. Their ground will of course again be the Nlesnes notwithstanding the rumours that they had received notice to vacate the ground. The most notable absentee from last season's ranks will be Dawson, the clever little centre forward, who has gone to Dar wen. Grime and Mills have also sought new hunting grounds, Bolton Wanderers having secured the services of both these promising players. Several new faces will be seen in the team, amongst Ithese being Hobin, the smart custodian who gave such a sterling display for Warrington against the locals last year. Andy Limond has also been induced to sign,whilst in place of Bartley at outside right, the services of a youth named Stanton late of Liverpool have been secured. The full team to choose from will be goalkeeper, Hobin ; backs, Leigh Cottam and Law- rence • balf backs, Lirnond, whitehouse, Pennington ; forwards. Stanton, Barlow, Tartan (late St, Helena Recs.) Leach and Settle. The Committee also have been alter a well-known centre forward who figured last season with one of the league clubs. Should his signa- ture be obtained, he wit' be a man every bit as good as Dawson to Earlestown. Earlestown have entered for both the Lancashire and Wigan Cups in addition of course to the English Cup. I trial match takes place on Saturday "and this will serve to show what sort of players the new men are. The members' cards are nowiready and the Secretary wishes all persons desirous of becoming members to apply for the same at once. Cho club have not had a very good members' list up to the present bat hope for a better list this season. A MARRIAGE AI- HILL CLIFFE.

On Tuesday afternoon there was a marriage in the ancient chapel at Hill Cliff which created no little interest in the neighbourhood,and there was a large com- pany of friends gathered to witness the ceremony at two o'clock; The contracting parties were Miss Worrall, of Birchdale, Stockton Heath, awl Mr. Alfred Reeves, Golbortte. TFe officiating minr was the past -it. (Rev J. Samuel Hughes. both Miss Worrall and Mr Reeves being members of the choir at Hill Cliffe. The organist (Mr. W. Hanes) WAS present, and played Wagner's " Bridal March " as the company asaem.hled, and Mendelseohn's " Weddiom March" at the close of the ceremony. The congregation also joined in singing two hymns "The voice that breathed o'er Edon," and " Since Jesus freely did appear to grace a marriage feast." The bride, who was given away by bar father, was charmingly attired in a dress of white silk, and was accompanied by two bridesmaids, Miss Reeves and Miss Hellas, the bridegroom having his brothe., Mr. A. Gibb Reeves as bost man. There were about thirty guests and numerous presents. On Friday night last week about forty friends con- nected with the Hill Chile Baptist Chapel met in social gathering in order to express their good wisbes to Miss Worrall and Mr Alfred Reeves, in prospect of their approaching marriage. After social fell )syship and refreshments there was a meeting, when the pastor, Rev J S Hughes, took the chair and spoke of the object of tha t pleasant which Mr Reeves and t,stified to the excellent nd Miss Worrell had rendered in Sunday echool, choir, and Y P S of Christian Endeav- our.tat service He expressed his sorrow at the prospect of losing them from the place, and the hops that in their united life, they would find haPuiciess and prosperity. Then he called unoo Mrs Hughes who in a few graceful words presented Miss Worrell with a beautiful china tea set, and a pair of silver jam spoons in case, on behalf of the teachers, young peoples society, choir and friends wishing her much happiness, Miss Worrell responded in a neat little speech thanking all for their kindness. Mr. Hughes then presented Mr Alfred Reeves with a teacher's Bible, on behalf of the same sozieties, and Mr Reeves responded in an excellent speech. Addresses were also delivered by Messrs E England, John Moss, Joseph Moss and William Wild, a recitation was given by Mr J. J. Worrell and a very pleasant evening was enjoyed.

div.head: Shaw before the Magistrates. The Case for floe Defence.
div.p: Shaw before the Magistrates. The Case for floe Defence.

Jsmcs Shaw, collier, aged forty-three, of Sutton Moss, was brought before the magistrates at S. Helens Town Hail on Thursday, charged with wilfully murdering Michael Nmuen, aged twenty-aloe, colliery banksman, of 2,1135 ck Berry'a-line, on tile night of the 5,n instant by shooting him. Mr W H Andr 3W, the recently appointed town-clerk, acted as prosecuting solicitor, and Mr U L Riley repre- sented Shaw. _ _ .

The tragedy, it may be remembered, took place in the presence of deceased'e brother' Thomas Neonen, who gave a very graphic description of the affair when before the Coroner. It appears that on the fatal night following August Bank Holi- day Monday, deceased and his brother and a friend named Alfred Johnson spent some time in the Boilermakers' Arms, Watery-lane, Sutton, where Shaw was also sitting drinking with three men named Thomas Tarpey, James Dixon, and Fred Gaiter. Whoe Shaw and his companions left the house, deceased is alleged to have hal a fight with some of t iem, and as he got the worst of the battle he went for his brother and Johnson. The three proceeded in the direction of Berry's-lane, but at the end of Rolling Mill-lane turned out of their way to follow Seaw and his party, the suggestion being that deceased was determined to have satisfaction for the boating he had received. After he and Dixon had gone threugh a somewhat serious bout, Shaw, who appears to have been little more than a spectator of the bother met the deceased and bis brother. He was carrying a gun, which was fired, whether wiJully or accidentally remains to be nroved, when the muzzle was only about a foot from Noonen's body. The shot entered the poor fellow's abdomen anl thigh, and he died about an hour and a half afterwaids. Tarpey says that he spent the greater part of the night with Shaw sitting under a haystack in the neighbourhood, and when day broke he walked with him to Warriagton. Shaw made his way to Koutsford, where his wife's mother resided, but on Wednesday evening returned home with her and was I arrested at his own house by Polic,-eonstable Marsh a little over twenty hours after the sad occurrence. Shaw displayed great calmness during the long ordeal °tithe coroner's inquiry, and contends that th 3 shooting was cot intentional and that the gun was exploded by Noonen's kicking his hands when they were all strug- gling for possession of the weapon. Mr Andrew, at to-day's proceedings, briefly detailed the circumstances of the tragedy. Thomas Noonen,brother of the murdered man,was the first witness canoe. He detailed the proceedings at the Boilermakers' Arms, and the order in which the men left the house, the quarrels between Dixon and deceased and the subsequent meetine with Shaw at the corner of Nook-lane. Shaw,to the beet of hiebelief,went away from the bother in the direction Of his house,presumably to fetch the gun. Shaw most deliberately poiuted the gun and shot his brother. When be was going away after witness had knocked him down, and the gun had been taken from him, Shaw said he would fetch another gun, and blow out tee brains of all three. Cross-examined by Mr Riley : He wo Id not swear that Shaw bad not the gun in his pocket when they were in the public-house. . . .

Witness would swear that the only struggling that took place for the gun was after the fatal shot bad been fired. None of them theught at the time that such seri- ous mischief had been done. He had never heard of his brother ever having had a quarrel with Shaw. The gun was only fired once. Alfred Ashton, collier, of 25, Watery-lane, spoke to going with Thomas Nomen altar deceased along Rolling Mill-iane. He saw the fights between Noonea and Hisao, Shaw was present at the beginning of the fight, but dis- appeared. Shaw afterwards met them at the corner of Nook-lane, and pu-, the gun to his shoulder, and, as he said, " Here's Shaw," he fired at Noonea. Shaw after- wards stood over the two men with the gun. Thomas Noonen knocked him down, and afterwards " ducked " when Shaw pointed it at him again,and knocked Shaw down again. Thomas said to him " Get bold of that gun, Alf," and witness snatched the gun out of Shaw's band when he wag on the floor.

_ By Mr Riley : Wnen Thomas left the public-house he said, "I cm going to follow our Mick up ; are you coming ?" and witness said, "I will." Taey both went , out to back Michael up. He would swear that Shaw left his mates before Thomas joined in the fray and knocked Gaiter down. Deceased did not go to the end of Nook- lane with the object of overtaking Shaw before he got home. He would swear that the struggling for the gun did not take place until after Noonen had been shot. He only beard one shot fired. James Dixon, colliery drawer, 28, Aelocroft-street, St Helens, said that he left the public house with Shaw. Michael Noonen folo wed them to the corner of Rolling Mill-lane and asked him to go back to the house,bulhe refused, and 'hey had a fight. Noonen went back, and witness went on with Suaw. When they got into Sutton Moss-lane Noonen came out of a ditch in froat of them, got hold of him, and started kickiag him. When he got up after this Shaw was away from them,and ha shortly afterwards saw prisoner about fifty yards away. He beard only one shot fired. Fred Gaiter said that be remembered nothing after Thomas Noouen knock 33 him down, until be found him- self on the cinder heap At Ashton's Green Colliery some hours aster. The previous day he was with Shaw with a dog and gun after hare.. Prisoner thee loaded both barrels. Seaw was quite able to conceal the gun in his pocket. Thomas Tarpey spoke to being knocbed down by Thomas Noonen. He heard one shot. When he got up he heard Shaw say, o, come again, come again." He saw several men wrestling, and a second shot rang out. Witness went towards the place an! saw Noonen lying on the ground. He heard the deceased talking to his brother, and then went to Shaw's house and joined Shaw, who said " There will be a bother just now; they ' will be after us." They therefore decided to go away for a few ho are. They went to the shelter of a peat stack until the break of day,after which they walked to Warrington. By Mr. Riley : When the struggle was going on there was no one lying on the ground. It must have been the second shot that did the mischief, and that went off when Shaw was struegling with the Neonens. During the night Shaw said that If the Noonens had not struggled for the gun no harm would have been done He said he dischareed it the first time in the hope of frightening them off. He showed marks on his hand where the skin had been kicked off be Tom Noonen when they were trying to ges the grin off him. Re-examined : after the first shot be heard Michael and Thomas Noonen talking, but be could not see them' The first shot might have done the mischief. Tnomae Critchley said that be beard one shot, and went along Nook-lane from his house, and found Noonen wounded. He did not hear a second shot. Police-constable Rigby said that when he heard of the occurrence he went to Sutton Moss and found Michrel Nommen ore the ground with about twenty or thirty people round him. Alfred Ashton handed him a gun. Both barrels were empty. Thera was a spent cap on the nipple of the right hand barrel. He recognised the gun as one that he had seen Shaw carrying on July 27. Dr. Unsworth spelce to attending the posleenortene with Dr Casey. Be described the shot wound in the groin, and said the charge had gone through in a slant- ing and backward direetkon down into the thigh. The muzzle must have been about a foot from the body.

By Mr Riley : If deceased was standing erect and was shot at point blank, he woull have expected a different result. The wound could not possibly have been produced by a charge fired straight at him at right angles. Mr Riley: If cleansed had been bending down, and engaged in a struggle, the possible results from such a position would more probably harmonise with what you found ? Dr Unsmorth : Quite. Mr Riley : Is it impossible that the shot was fired at so great a distance as eight or nine yards away? Dr Unswortn : To my mind, quite impossible. Witne.ss further said it was impossible to ascertain, owing to the clothing being saturated with bl3od, if there was any scorching or marks of powder on the trousers. . _

Dr Casey said he was called to deceased after he was shot-. Next, day he made the post-mortem. The cause of death was hemorrhage, and shock fto it the gunshot wound. Judging from the sivi of the wound, the gun was more than a foot away from deceased's body. There was no burning about the clothing or the wound. Police-constable Richard March said that when he was conveying prisoner to the police station afte. the arrest, Shaw said, "It wasn't ma whq, shot him, it was his brother. lam sorry he is dead. There was a struggle, and me and Tarpey went to Warringt en this morning, and Tarpey left ms there." Inspector Steel gave evidence after Police-constable Littler, and said that on the day after the arrest he ex- amined prisoner's hands, and found skin off two cf the knuckles. Waiter G Nexth, assistant ironmonger, said the tight- hand barrel of Soaves gun had h-en fired recently, but the left-hand barrel had not biien fired for a considerable time. The Town-clerk said that was the case for thsi prosecu- tion, whereupon Mr Riley said that if the magistrates would charge Shaw he was prepared to make a state- ment.

div.head: SHAW DESCRIBES WHAT HAPPENED.
div.p: SHAW DESCRIBES WHAT HAPPENED.

Shaw then read as follows :—I have not much to say. I loaded up the gun,and had been out with it the morn- ing before, but never got a shot ; and I intended going out ag in en the Tuesday night and waiting for day- light. I put the gun in my inside pockets, one piece in each pocket, and I dsresay I was a bit careful that nobody should see I', because this summer I have not taken out a licence to carry a gun. I had taken them out in previous years, but my last one ran out on the 31st of last July, just fin dips before. I knew Rigby would be on the I ookont. Re knew I bad not renewed my licence. When the N oonens and Ashton followed ma fold my mates, and Dixon and Gaiter and Tarpey were all on the ground together, I thought I would leave them at it, and went

towards borne. Somebody called out something about me, and the next I saw was the Noonens and Ashton following me up. I was still 150 yards, more or less, sway from home. I bad been laid up with rbeumaeism, and was in no fit fettle for fighting ; so as I saw them ; coming I fired my gun into the air. One of teem.eitber , Michael Noonen or Thomas, called out, " We will have thee. And thy --gun, too." They rushed towards me, and we commenced struggling. Thomas Noonen hit me twice on my forehead, and k;cked Ime on the right band twice, trying to get get the gun off me. Michael Noonen got hold of it, too and it was in this straggle it went off and shot Michael There would not have been above flee minutes between the two shots. I never aimed the gun point blank at Michael, and I never wanted to moot either him or any- body elm. I have never been a man for using violence. All there is against me is taking a drop of arink now and again, and doing a bit of poaching. I came back to give myself up as soon as I heard anything serious had happened. I went to Warrington and on to limits- ford, unknowing that Noonen was dead, and thinking there wouli be more bother next day if I stopped at home. I have relations at Kautsford, and I otten go over there _ . _

Mr Riley addressed the court, and said the prisoner's story was supported in every way, and he trusted that the magistrates would give Shaw the satis- faction of appearing at the Assizes, backed up with the knowl,‘dge that two magistrates had come to tho conclu- I Mon that the accident theory bad preponderated over the theory of wilful shooting, The magistrates retired for three or four minutes, when Colonel M'Tear said : After careful consideration, we think that this i a case that ought to be tried by a jury. We therefere commit the prisoner to be tried at the neat assiz3s on the charge preferred against him. The hearing concluded at twenty minutes Co eight, having commenced ot 11 a.m. During the whole of the day a large crowd waited in front of the Town Hall.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNCILLORS Al BUXTON.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNCILLORS Al BUXTON.

Mr S Taylor, IP., chairman of the Runcorn Urban District Council,on Wednesday took his fellow members, ' who have delighted to honour him by placing him as their president on several occasions, a " trip" to Buxton. A number of Mr Taylor's personal friends were also in- vited. The party travelled from Runcorn in a specially chartered saloon corridor train, which left Runcorn at 8,30 a.m. A stoppage of two hours was made at Dore Holes, a hamlet set in the midst of Derbyshire hills and dales, where Mr Tayl n's extensive lime works were in- spected. The in 7stories of lime quarrying were explored with zest and enjoyment, and a wonderful machine for crushing and separating the stone into seven different sizes for road making purposes, met with due attention. The tour was made wider Mr Taylor's personal guidance and his crisp explanations added much to the instruc- tion of the visitors. The " Special "was again boarded and B,lx x:•ri quickly reached. A high class dinner was splendidly served at the Palace Hotel, where Mr Taltlor naturally occupied the post of honour and Mr J M Frith was the vice-chairman, The Chair- man gave the usual loyal toasts in his orn whole hearted breezy style and then Dr McDougall pro- posed the health of the host. The worthy doctor in- vested this toast with all the charm which his sincere oratory always bestows, with a few added touches of humour. Be showed that Runcorn people were honoured by Mr Taylor living among them and accepting public service at their bands. Mr Taylor's kindness, sympathy and hospitality knew no bounds. Time was too short too extol Mr Taylor's many virtures. The toast was ably supported by Mr Seatrue and Mr Lea of Liverpool and was rece:vs d with great enthusiasm. Mr Taylor made a characteristic reply, in which he directed attention from his own merits to the beauties of Buxton and said no guest was enjoying ;himself more fully than he himself was. His sorrow was that the circumstances of life did not admit of their meeting oftener under such happy conditions. The Chairman then proposed the health of Mr A. Brown, chairm in of Buxton Urban District Council, and this gentleman acknowledged the compliment i a appropriate terms and afterwards conducted the party over the public works of Buxton. These Included. sewage, water, electricity, hospitals, Ste., and needless to say proved of great interest to the Cheshire visitors. Runcorn was safely reached at 8 p.m.

div.head: LATE LATE CAPTAIN WILLIS.
div.p: THE LATE LATE CAPTAIN WILLIS.
Adjourned Inquest and Verdict.

On Thursday, before Mr T E Sampson, in the City Coroner's Court. Liverpool, an inquiry, adjourned from last week, was held in reference to the death of Captaia H H d'Anyers Willie, of Halanead Hall, Preece% aged sixty-eight years, which occurred in a railway carriage on a journey from Wigan to Liverpool, on Wedeesday, 13th inst. The Coroner informed the jary at the commencement of the sitting that the matter appeared to have become much simplified since the adjournment, as it was under- stood that medical evidence would be given, showing that if the deceased had received any personal injury, it had nothing to do with toe cause of hei death. The Rev. J Brown, rector of D.cicct oafish, Berkshire, brother-in-law of the deceased, was the first witness, He knew that Captain Willis was suffering from heart disease. WAness and Captain Willis had made an arrangement that the first-named should meet witness at the railway station with his carriage, but th st was cancelled owing to the carriage having been damaged in an accident on the 2nd instant. When witness got to Halinead Hall he found Captain Willis in the midst oi a school treat, ap- parently in his usual health, but complaining of a little tenderness about the head. 03 the previous Monday when being driven to Lend Gerard's funeral hie carriage had been run into by a St Helens tramcar which left the metals at the points. The coachman was knock- ed off,and as the horses were without the driver,Captain Willis thought he had better get out. He got upon the carriage-step and jumped clear of the door, but fell and hurt his head. Toe day after the arrival of witness Captain Willis gave a dinner party and seemed to be perfectly well and cheerful. Next morning he went to Preston t) attend a County Council meeting, and next Monday he heard of his death. Mr Joseph Harrison, stationmaster, Edge-bill, (formerly of Latchford), gave evidence that on the afternoon of Wednesday, the 13th inst., he saw Captain Willis, whom he had known for e ire, lying in a first. class compartment of a train which had just airived from Wigan. He seemed to he reclining in a peculiar position, with his right side on the seat. Witness found that he was quite dead. Leaving him in the compart- ment, witness sent an inspector on with the train, and meantime telephoned to Limo-street to make arrange- ment, and went down himself by a subsequent train, The Coroner.—l understand that you wish te say something regarding comments made by irresponsible people, not conversant with the requirements of the law about not sending the body back to Wigan. I think it right to say that you acted quite properly, and that had you done as these people suggested,you would have rendered yourself liable t be dealt with for contempt of court. Police-constable 237 testified to having been sent for and having found the dead body in a first-class carriagc. Dr House gave evidence as to seeing the dead body in the railway carriage, and regarding the results of a post- mortem examination made at the city coroner's request. A very careful examination of the head revealed neither external not internal marks of violence.tut the heart was found to be extensively diseased, and about double the normal weight. He ascribed death to failure of the ha art's action, being quite satiefied that any injury the deceased might have sustained recently o at any other time had nothing whatever to do with the cause of death. Corroborative evidence was given by another practitioner. The Coroner, in summing up, took occasion to refer to the responsibility which the station-mister would have incurred in taking upon himself to remove the body oqt of the jurisdiction in which it was found. He had had many years' experience of Mr Harrison and the careful way in which he did everything. A verdict of " Death from natural Causes " was returned. Mr Arkle, solicitor, speaking on behalf of Captain Willis's family, said that they never imputed any blame to the station-master. Mr G Magee (Hill, Dickinson, and Co) watched the interests of the Sc Helens Tramways Company.

rhe Proposed Electric Express Railw.ay• Surveys were made on Wednesday in the Irlam and Cadishead districts in connection with the pro- posed electric express railway between Manchester and Liverpool. It is hoped the construction will shortly be commenced; and, when the work is finished, it is expected that the journey will be , made in eighteen minutes. The railway may be completed early in 1904. Sale of Latchford Property. Messrs John Mainwaring and Company offered for sale by auction at the Blue Bell Inn, Horse- market-street, on Wednesday evening, two freehold ' dwelling-houses and building land at Latchford There was a good attendance,and after some s irit- ed bidding, lot 1, consisting of two fre 'hold dwelling houses, with the gardens thereto, known as Bryn Felin Villas, situate near Lamb lirook, in Chester-road, Latchford Without,was sold for ..EGGS. Lots 2 and 3 consisted of plots of freehold building land,containing 1,500 and 1,519 square yards respec- tiveiy, and they tound a purchaser at £370. Mr T J Ridgway, 2, Cairo-street, was solicitor to the vendors.

"Amongst the recent arrivals in Cipe Town" says the Cape Times," "is Mr Edward Porritt, a distin- guished English journalist who has come to South Africa upon a special mission for the great trade paper,' Commercial Intelligence.' Mr Porritt, who has been all over the world upon similar commis- sions for impovant British jmirnals, expects to spend some months in South Africa studling the economic conditions of the country, its require- ments, and the openings for British manufactures.' Local Oddfellowship. The fortnighly meeting of the Loyal Friendship Lodge No 1087 was held at the "Green Dragon" Inn, Bridge-street,on Monday evening. There was a very good attendance of members and visiting brethren. N G William Bowness was in the chair and V G Oswald Peacock in the vice-chair, sup- ported by the following offilers :—G M James Bramhall, D G I Walter Duncan (Elrlestown), D. Secretary Thomas Dickinson, juu, P P G M's Long- shaw, Hands and Pester; and P• G's Charaley, Daniels, Kelly, Pennington,and Burgess (secretary. After the usual business of the lodge had been transacted, DG M Walter Duncan presented an emblem of merit to P U William Pennington for services rendered. Bro Duncan said it gave him much pleasure to be called upon to perform so pleasing a duty, and spoke in eulogistic terms of the able manner in which Bro Pennington had gone through the chairs of the lodge. Congratulatory speeches were given hy Bros Bramball, Longshaw, Hands. and Paster, and the recipient thanked the members for their handsome present, and said he would do his utmost in support of Oddfellowship and the "Friendship Lodge in particular.

GARL &ND. Ironmonger, Bridge-st, Warrington."—Advt. BLOT BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDICR THE CLOCK.—Advt Lymm Boy Run Over and Killed. Mr Dobson conducted an inquiry at the Farmer's Arms, Lymm, on Saturday afternoon, concerning the death of George Andrew Briars, the eight-year- old son of the landlord. On Thursday, the 14tO Inst., the deceased and a boy named Jesse Percival, went with a man named William Morton to Stretton for a lorry load of hay. At Stretton Morton placed the deceased's overcoat in the sheet box, which is situated in the centre of the under part of the lorry. All went well until Curry-lane, Lymm, was again reached, at which point Morten was leading the horses, while the boys were walking on the off-side of the vehicle. Dia deceased went between the wheels for the purpose of getting his coat, when he fell and the back wheel of the vehicle pasted over the top part of his legs. The horses were going slowly at the lime. A trap came up, in which Morton placed the boy, and he was taken to Dr Brabazon'A. It was then decided to take him to the Warrington Infirmary but as he died on the journey there,he was taken home azain Death took place about an hour after the unfortun- ate accident. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and said the driver Morton was in no way to blame. They expressed their sympathy with the bereaved family. St. Paul's Choir Trip. . .

_... .- On Saturday the adult members ot St Paul's choir, accompanied by the Vicar and Mrs Bracecamp, Mr E Wilkes (organist) and Mrs Wilkes, Councillor and Mrs Brough, Miss Westwell, mission lady, and several other friends, altogether to the number of about 45, bad their annual trip,Llangollen being the resort visited. Special carriages were attached to the 817 train, and, alter a very pleasant run, the attractive old town was reached at about ten o'clock. The weather being of an ideal character, the sun shining throughout the day, enabled the visitors to spend about nine hours in the open. It was decided to open the tour of inspection by a visit to the Horse Shoe Falls at Berwyn, and for this purpose one of the large canal boats was requisitioned. Toe beautiful scenery excited the admiration of all and the pleasure of the party was considerably enhanc- ed by the vocal efforts of the choir,who sang several anthems in a highly creditable manner. Some of the party walked back to town, to enable them to. obtain a better view of the scenery than was pos- sible from the boat, but all assemble,' at twelve o'clock at the Hotel Royal, where an excellent and well-served dinner was provided. At the close the Vicar gave the toast of " The Ring " ( which was warmly received), The party then started on their walk to Crow. Castle, a conical bill 1.000 feet high an the north ' side of the town, but finding a suitable sp 'it on a hillock just beyond the canal a halt was made to enable Mr Hindley, a member of the choir, ta take a photograph of the party, which turned out to be successful. Later on the visitors paid a visit to IPhis Newydd, now a charming show house, but the whilom residence of the eccentric " Ladies of Llan- gollen." and also inspected and had a rest in the ' pretty Parish Church,enishing up their labours with a ramble alona the river-ide on the way to Berwyn. At six o'clock all again met at the hotel for tea,

which, after the lonv, afternoon spent in the open, was found to bs very welcome and refreshing. After visiting other places of interes•.; in the town the party wended their way to the station. Here some other glees were rendered in first-clivs style, until the train steamed into the station and the beautiful, but not easily fortsotten pleasure resort was soon left far behind. Warrington was reached at 9.30,and there was a consensus of opinion that a more enjoyable day in the history of the kchoir trips has yet to be rezardsd

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

FAILING To NOTIFY SCARLET FEVER OASES. At the Warrington Borough Police Court yesterday, before Mr He..heri and other magistrates, Abraham Dykes. of 5. Richardson's-row. Liverpool-road, was summoned for failing to notify infectious disease.—Mr Stanley Wilson (deputy Town Clerk) prosecuted, and stated that the circumstances were about as bad as they could be, because no doctqr had been called in, From information which Inspector -Flood received on July 29th. be visited the defendants house in company with the Medical Officer of Health. They found a child seven years of age, suffering from scarlet fever and in a peeling stage. The mother stated that she noticed a rash on the Bth July. Another child, aged 5, was also suffering from the same disease. No doctor bad been called In and one or the children—a boy—had been playing with other children in the neighbourhood and had been in the habit of taking his father's meals to the works of Messrs Monks, Hall and Company. If parents neglected their duties in this way it was little use the Corporation spending large sums of money in providing and maintaining an infectious diseases hospital. It was the simplest thing in the verrld to eallln a doctor and get the case certified to the Medical Officer of Health. There was no doubt the mother was aware of what the child was sufferiog from. There had been a slight epidemic o'r scarlet fever in this district and it was in all probability due to the non-notification of the disease through the negligence of parents. The magistrates fined the defendant 511 including costs.—Peter Gleave, 46, Liverpool-road and John Moran 19. Piekmere-street were each tined 4s 6d costs for a like offence atthe Borough Court on Friday last w,ek. THREE MONTHSWARD LsEOUR FOR WOVE BEATING. At the Borough Police Court on Saturday, before Mr T Birchall (presiding, and Dr Fm, a carter named William Caldwell, 4 Hart's-place. Bridge-street, pleaded guilty to an aggravated assault on his wife, Martha Elizabeth Caldwell.— Mr Steel, who prosecuted on behalf of complainant, said he was informed the latter was a very decent, hard working respectable woman. whilst her husband was a drunken lazy wastrel. He spent the hard earnings of his wife in drink. For some time he had been hanging about doing no work. On Wednesday night complainant had to lock I her bedroom door, and her two sons stayed up to protect her. Prisoner got up about 7.30 on Thursday morning and went out. His wife then locked Loth the front and back doors. Prisoner subsequently returned and climbed over the back door. He shouted "Are you going to let me in ?" They were afraid to let him in, and he picked up a shevel and broke five panes of glass in the win- dow. He forced his way into the house, and rushed at his wife, threatening to murder her. tile used violence, bat one of the sons just prevented a further aseault. The police records showed that prisoner had served several terms of imprisonment for wife assault, and two separation orders had been made against him, the last one in October, 1887. Complainant put the house In her own name. Prisoner even- tually over-persuaded her to lev. him live with her again, but she had not had much comfort since.—Complainant corrobora- ted this statement. She asked the Bench to convict prisoner of an eggravated assault in order that she might have a separation. She was afraid to live with him.— Prisoner said be had four grasses of beer on Thursday. and somebody put something in one of them which upset him (Laughter.)—The Chairman : There is always something of that kind.—Prisoner said he was sorry to be in that position, and if the Bench and his wife would be kind enough to look over the offense he would sign the pledge—Complainant said prisoner had promised to do that before, and she had no faith in bim.—Sunerintendent Monaghan stated that this was prisoner's 10th appearance. He had been four times to gaol for assaulting his wife. the lest time for three months. —The Bench remarked that some men thought that wives were just for to be knocked about anyway. Prisoner would have to go to goal for three months, and a separation order would be granted, prisoner to cOntriblite Is a week towards the maintenance of his wife and two children aged eight and ten.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
Warrington Borough Court.

FRlDAY—Before Mr Hepherd (chairman), Counoillor Smethurst, Councillor John Roberts and air H Thornton. THEFT FROM AN OYSTER DEALER'S HOUSE.—Sarah Hunt, a stranger In the town, was charged with stealing a quantity of ladies clothing value 3s from the premises of Joseph Cann, oyster dealer,22,WinWick-street.—Superintendent Monaghan stated the case and the magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for 14 days hard labour. A BRUTAL HUSRAND.—Edward Mee, of 26, Stevenson. street, was charged with assaulting and beating his wife, Ellen Mee on the 2nd of August,— The complainant stated that her husband struck her on the head with his fist. She I ran outside and whilst standing at the door he threw a loaf, a coat. some cups and saucers and a lighted lamp at her. The defendant denied striking his wife and stated that his Wife annoyed him by 6. drinking and muffing" with neighbours. He Was lined 20s including costs or 14 days imprisonment. Two flows IN SHARP-STREET.—Louisa Hargreaves, of 88. Bbarp-street. was summoned on a charge of assaulting John Hussey, of 8,5, Sharp-street on the 9th August.—The com- plainant, who appeared in Court with a wnind over the left eye said the defendant, without any provocation, struck him a violent blow over the eye.—The defendant, who was very demonstrative in the box and had to be warned by the magistrates, denied the charge and said it was "a made up thing among 'em," Sho was fined les and costs. On hearing the magistrates' decision she remarked "You are not getting any money out of me,,' and WRS immediately taken down to the cells below.—Mrs Miller, of 83 Sharp-street was summoned on a charge of assaulting Sarah Hussey. wife of the complainant in the last case, on the Bth Inst. The defendant pleaded "guilty to biting her in self defence." The complainant stated that the defendant bit her on the hand and she had to have it bathed for an hour—Mrs Whitby gave corroborative evidence, and stated that after the defendant received the summons on :Monday she "carried on " In the street and threatened to bite the complainant's head off.—The defendant said she had forgiven the complainant for hitting her in the face with a wet stocking and for abusing her on other occasions. On the date named Mrs Hussey pulled her hair snd dragged her down. Mr Hussey and his eon also assaulted hen—She was fried us including coats.

SATURDAY—Before Mr. Birchall (in the chair) and Dr rox. Dauxx.—John Kelly, a- hawker, of Bennett-street, was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk and disorderly on Friday.—P.O. Casey proved the case. ' ABSOCCSDING ' YR°NI THE WoRYHOUBE.-41, stranger named Edward Taylor was committed to prison for seven days for absconding from the Workhouse at 5 50 that morning, before he had perfermed his task.—Prisoner said he wanted to get On the road to look for work. COAL STEAM:NO.—John Rose, 12, Eldon-street, pleaded guilty to stealing llevrt of coal, of the value of is, from a yard at Longford Wire Works.—Superintendent Monaghan stated that the defendant was ft labourer and had been in the emplOyl of the Corporation for 27 years. At seven o'clock that morning Constable Lewis was In Kerfoot-street, and raw the defendant wheeling a barrow laden with coal. coming from the directiOn of the wire works. He followed him and subsequently questioned him as to what he had done with the coal. He said he had got it from the engineer at the Longford Wire Works, and had taken It home. Lewis made Inquiries and found that this statement was not true. On being charged he said " Yes, I took it."—The Bench said they were sorry to see the man who so far had been fairly respectable, in such a position. They would, however, give him a chance. and he would be fined lOs and costs, RI 9s. or In default 14 days' imprisonment. MONDAY.—Before Mr Birchall (in the chair), Councillor Smethurst. and Messrs 3 Wright and Henry Thornton. DRUNKENNESS.—The following were fined for drunkenness —Samuel Clifton, 10, Portland-street ; Martin Rogers. a stranger; Daniel Ghagan, of no settled abode, and Michael Mulligan, 2'. Brwood-street. A JOINER'S MAINTENANCE ARREARS—WiIIiam joiner, was charged on a warrant for arrears of maintenance and costa due to his wife amounting to RS 17s 6d•—Mr Steel 'represented the wife and the defendant was represented by Mr Crompton. —Mr Steel said that an order was made in 1901 for the defengant to contribute 12s a week for the mainten- ance of his wife and child. He had been very aregular in his payments, as the amount of the arrears would show. Defendant was In a very good pocition, he being is partner- ship with his father as a builder, and quite able to pay the money.—Mr Crompton contended that the payments had been made very regularly. and there could be no suggestion that the wife and child had suffered by reason of the arrears. The defendant's wife and child lived at Birmingham with her mother. The arrears were the result of the many holidays. He offered to par the 12s and is a week extra to to clear off the amount.—Mr Steel did not think this was sufficient.—An

order was made for defendant to pay 24 down and 2s per week to clear off the arrears.—Mr Crompton disputed the amount stated as being due and the Bench fixed it at £B. DRUNK IN C9UBT.-loseph Garrett and Maria Garret, 2, Morris's-court ; and James and Sarah Ann Medley, of the • same address, were all charged with baying been drank and disorderly in Morris's-court, on the 11th August. The two first defendants were drunk, and the Chief Constable re- quested that they should be remanded in custody until Tuesday, by whica time, be said, they would be sober. This was &me, and the ease against the other two defendants pro- ceeded.--P.O. Bruen stated the facts, and defendants were each fined 2s 6d. On Tuesday. Joseph Garrett and Maria Garrett were again placed in the dock and were fined 2s 6d each. ABUSIVE LANGIIAGE.—For having used abusive language in Dial-street. on August 13th, Bridget Wheeler 2, Jolley's- c mrt, was fined be and costs.
WRDNESDAY.—Eefore Aldermen Hutchinson (In the chair)
ad Monk e.

THEFT FROM BEwsav FORGE.—Robert Kirk. Railway-view, Padgate, was charged with stealing a perambulator wheel and two pieces of scrap iron, of the value of 6d, the property of Messrs Pearson and Knowles, Bewsey Forge, —lnspe&or Phillips said prisoner was a paddler at Bewsey Forge. where he had bees employed for the last four years at a salary of EZ a week. About five o'clock that morning Comstable Sweeney was on duty in Orford-lane, when he met tho prisoner carrying something under his arm. The ofilnr stopped him and asked what it was. Prisoner replied that it was an old perambulator wheel and that he had been constantly taking things of that kind from the forge. Prisoner was taken to the polis Station, where two other pieces of scrap iron were found in his possession. The authorities at the Forge were com- municated with, and they stated that prisoner bad no right to take the material. They had missed a considerable quantity of scrap Iron from the works for i. long time.— Prisoner admitted the theft and was fined 10s and costs (19e in all), or 14 days' imprisonment.

WARRINGTON MEN FINED FOR TRF?9PASSLNG IN SEARCH OF GAME.—Mark Phipps and John Warren. Antrotus-street, Winwick-road, We rringtonovere charged with trespassing on land in the occupation of Isaac Joseph Howard of Houghton, li, search of game.—Mr Longton said he appeared to prose- cute on bahalf of Mr J W Knowles, who had the shooting rights of the land, ana the tencult. Mr Howard. On August 4th defendants were seen in a clover field at Ho•lgh- ten with a small dog. They were apparently beating the field in search of game. The men were some ten yards trona each other and between 300 and 300 yards from any footpath. Their method of procedure mould lead any one to understand that they were after game. Warren gave a wrong name and address, and told the constable that they were not friends and did not know each other. As a matter of fact they lived in the same street, and were evidently together.—Constable Callaghan gave evislewe.—Phipps stated that he was lyine. asleep in the field, and Warren said he went into the field to waken him. Both defendants denied being in search of game —They were each fined lOs and costs. ASSAULT.—Joshua Meredith was summoned for assaulting Percy Croughton at Poulton on the 11th inst.—Corapi4nant stated that he was walking from the direction of Warrington when defendant ran oat of a farm yard and hit him ea beth sides of the face.—Fined 5s and costs.

OTHER Oriddcde, —John Lythgoe was fined 6s and cuts fer being drunk in charge of a horse and furry at Pounce on the 13th Inst.—William Morris was fined Is and costs for riding a bicycle on the !footpath at Monghton on the 10th inst.—Richard Cooper was summoned for eemmitting a breach if the peace at Croft by fighting on the Zrd last.—lie was bound over to keep the peace.

div.p: Warrington Occasional Court.
SATITIRDA.Y.—Before Mr. F A Frost.

ALLEGED TAM? OF TRON.—agnes Clynes, Winifred Bnoc- ton, and James O'Brien were charged with stealing a quantity of iron the property of Messrs Heenan and Fronde, bridge builders.---Evidence was given by P.O. Hayes to the effect that the women and the boy were carrying something heavy in a bag on the river bank, and Ciynes was wheeling a carriage containing iron. When they observed the officer was following them they left the carriage and threw the bag of iron over some railings in a stonemason's yard near Axpley Station. The boy was asked by the women to help them to carry the iron, Clynes and Knocton were remanded to Dares- bury Petty Sessions, while tha boy was discharged.
Runcorn Petty Sessions.
MONDAY-84f ore Memo F 3 Norman and W Timm.

I VACCINATION BxEMPFION.—Harry Hewitt applied for a vaccination exemption certificate In respect of his son John Wilson Hewitt, who was born on the 251 h Hay. The appli- cant objected to take the oath and affirmed. He stated his conscientious "belief that vaccination would prejudice his child's life and the certificate was granted. STONE THROWING.—John Doyle (11), of Water-street was summoned for throwing stones in Mersey-street on the 2nd Augnst.—P.O. Preston deposed that one stone almost struck a child on the head.—Superintendent Hanlon said the de- fendant bad previously been brought to the police station by a gentleman for breaking a window by stone throwing.---A fine of to was imposed. RABIES ONDER.-0a the evidence of Superintendent Ennion, Thom AS Allman of Vine-yard, we. fined 5. for allow- ing his dog to be at large without collar. or muzzle_ . _

THE YOUNG HOUSEBREAKER. —Minnie Birkenhead, aged 11 years.of Dutton Lodge Cotters sv-is charged with stealing a variety of sliver articles value £1 81 fid, the property of Maria Metcalf, of Aston Orange. The prisoner had spent a week under remand at Dutton Workhouse. Mr Norman said it was a very difficult case to deal with, but after full consideration the Bench had decided to bind prisoner over under the First Offenders' Act. _ _ _ _ .

- Fatilin BY • BOT.—Peter Sankey. aged 14 years. of aranville-street, was charged with stealing 9,1 by means of a triek from William Banks, joiner, &a, High- street. Mr Banks said the boy had been in his employ two or three weeks. On Thursday the 14th inst he sent him to Mr Crosby's,Top Locks,for a score of bran and a score of chcp,and handed him 2s3d to pay for the goods When the boy returned he was suspicious that he had not brought the proper quantity and he sent him back for a bill. The prisoner went away and coming back, said Mr Crosby had no bill and that he was to go next morning and witness found that the stufil was more than 10lbs short.—Mr W T Crosby, bay and corn merchant, spoke to prisoner ordering 151los of chop and 101bs of bran ; and witness gave him a bill and the change. Afterwards the prisoner came and asked Mr Arthur Crosby for a pennyworth of bill heads, but ha was told he could not have them. It Was a practice amongst toys to order less than they were sent for and to pocket the difference.—P S Gregory gave evidence of apprehension,The prisoner admitted his guilt.—Mr Norman said the prisoner had started in a very bad way. The Bench would not fine him because this would tall upon his parents. He would receive nine strokes-of the rod. . _

div.head: CYCLE PARADE & CARNIVAL.'
div.p: CYCLE PARADE & CARNIVAL.'
Another Meeting of Ladies.

Considerable enthusiasms is being disolived by th ladies who have undertakm the task of collecting. On Monday evening the secretsrirs in charge of the ladies' section called a further meeting, and the response was most encouraging. Considerably °wt. 100 collectGrs put in an appearance, and the seating accommodation of the Council Chamber at the Town Hall was taxed to its utmost. Mr D Davies, the chairman of the Commit- tee, was accompanied by Messrs E Pickavanco, general secretary ; R H Evans, J C Robinson, and ,C Leigh.

At the outset Mr DAVIE 3 informed the ladies ttat the Mayoress was unable Co be present being out of town. Miss Ditchfield had kindly consented to take the chair. Continuing, he said the committee desired him to thank the ladies for their kindness in coming forward in such numbers. If there was one thicg which gave the com- mittee more encouragement than another it was the presence of so many ladies,who showed such willingness to take part in the parade. It possible, the attendance was larger that iliglat than a fortnight ago, which was very gratifying. Be gave the collectors instructions as to taking the collections, &C. Mr PICICAVANCE said he had received a very kind note from the Mayoress saying that she hoped they would require a very large number of her photographs for the collectors.

----- Mr D/Ivigs said he would like, by request of the com- mittee, to urge upon the ladies to persevere in their efforts, and to remember that they were engaged in a very noble work—a work which, he might say, WSJ par- ticularly a woman's work, and there wax no lady in the Empire who took a greater interest in such work than did their Gracious Queen, so that they were following a splendid example. He thanked them for their attend- ance and support and also thanked Miss Ditch field for kindly coming forward and taking the chair. Miss DITCHrIELD said she hoped Saturday's parade would be a great success. She thought if they worked hard they would get in a lot of money, as the people of Warrington were very generous. The following ladies were appointed to the fixed town stands, which proved such a large source of revenue in 1900 :—Palmyra-square, Misses Thompson and Barker ; Bank Quay Station, Miss Darbyshire and friend ; Central I I Station, Misses Baldry ; Market-place, Misses Lawton and Renshaw ; Trinity Church, Misses Taylor ; Bridge- street tram terminue, Mrs Forbes and Miss Isherwood ; Bridge-street 'bus terminus,Misses Williams and Turner; Bridge Foot, Miss Knight and Mrs Powell ; Scotland. road, Misses Whittaker and Turner ; Post Office, Misses Ditchfie Id,

div.head: MARRIAGE AT BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHURCH.
div.p: MARRIAGE AT BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHURCH.
Richardson—Perkins.

A large congregation assembled in Bold-street Wesleyan Church, Warrington, on Tuesday after- noon to witness the marriage of Mr Levi Richard- son, son of Mr Peter Richardson, and Miss Florence Perkins, daughter of the late Mr W S Perkins, of Walton. The officiating ministers were the Revs 1 T Bishop and T Gunnell. The bride,who was given away by her brother, wore an ivory satin dress and ore Rialto veil (specially made by Mrs Jones, Liverpool-road). She also wore a pearl brooch, the gift of the bridegroom, and carried a bouquet of stephanotis, lilies, and white heather. She was attended by four brides- maids Miss Ettie Perkins (sister of the bride), Miss Emily Burgess (niece of the bridegroom),Miss Katie Looney (Peel), and Miss Frances Allen, who wore dresses of cream alpaca trimmed with lace and chiffon, with black picture bats. They carried bouquets of roses the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr J Barlow discharged the duties of best man. Mr Frank Hickman presided at the organ with his customary ability, and while the guests were as- sembling played "Chanson Busse " (smith), "Caprice " (Guilmant), "March Nuptiale" (Guil- mant), and "My heart ever faithful " (Bach). A select choir was in attendance and effectively rendered the anthem " 0 gladsome light." The hymn" The voice that breathed o'er Eden" was also sung. At the conclusion of the cere- mony the o,ganist played Mendelesohn'e "Wedding March " and the" Bridal March " from " Lolsengrin A reception was subsequently held in the adjoining schoolroom which had been tastefully decorated by Messrs G and J Weaver, and a large number of guests were received by Mrs Perkins, the bride's mother. The catering was in the able hands of Miss Ashurst. The wedding cake was made by Mr Meecbam of Norfolk, Later in the day the newly- married couple left for a tour in Devonshire, amid hearty*cengratulations.
