div.head: PRESENTATION TO vvESLEVAN MINISTERS.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO vvESLEVAN MINISTERS.
Farewell Addresses.

The Rev Theodore Bishop (superintendent of the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit) and the Rev C Hale Hocken(minister of Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church) have each completed three years' service in War- rington, and in accordance with the usual practice in the Wesleyan denomination they have departed for another sphere of labour. On Sunday last, they preached farewell sermons to their respective con- gregations and were the recipients of presents.

div.head: AT BOLD-STREET.
div.p: AT BOLD-STREET.

Prior to the evening service at Bold-street Wes- leyan Church, the members of the Wesley Guild assembled in the Ministers' Vestry f,-)r the purpose of wishing " God speed " to the Rev Theodore Bishop and presenting him with a small token of their love and esteem. When Mr. Bishop arrived three years ago the Guild was not then in a flourish- ing condition, but by his indefatigable efforts, kindly personality, and whale-hearted sympathy with the members, he has raised it to one of the best conducted and most successful Guilds in Me'hodism.

Mr G. BRAN presided over a very representative assembly of the Guild. After prayer The CHAIRMAN said they had assembled to say an revoir to their esteemed president Mr Bishop, In accordanre with the inexorable laws of the Wesleyan Church three years was the limit with which they could expect to be favoured with one minister, and Mr. Bishop had come- to the end of his term, end he was leaving for another sphere of labour. They would miss him very much. They would miss his manly and his many-sided Christianity. They would also miss him for the deep interest which he had taken in every phase of their work. When they fully realized he was going they thought they would like to offer him some tangible token of their esteem and regard, so that he might have something before him to remind him of his happy associations in his Guild work in War- rington. The movement was taken up most heartily. They were there to wish him "God- speed" and give him the tokens of their very high esteem and regard.. . . _ _

Mr R H SUTTON also spoke in appreciation of Mr Bishop's work. Although he had not known him as long as most of them had, as he (Mr Sutton) had only been in Warrington twelve months, he would. like on that occasion to thank Mr Bishop on his own behalf for the hearty welcome be gave him to Warrington. He was sure they all regretted their superintendent was about to leave them. He took a kindly interest in them and was a friend of the Guild movement. They all wished him "God-speed" in his new sphere of labour, and hoped he would be enabled to do more if possible for the Guild in hii new church than he had done for them in Warring- ton.

Mrs LITTLER then presented Mr Bishop with a gold " Wesley Guild" badge and a "Tennyson Birthday Book," in the latter of which the names of the Guild members were inscribed. In making the presentation she said the Guild badge and the birth- day book were a small token of the esteem and love in which Mr ishop was held,and their good wishes went with him. They hoped that wherever he came in touch with a Wesley Guild he might have the same love which existed at Warrington between himself and the members.

Mr F Lanrrlalso spoke. Mr Bishop, he said, always took a great interest in their sports,and they woull miss him very much. The Rev T BISHOP, who was much affected,said he did not think it was necessary to give him anything for the work he bad done. It had had its own reward, and it had been a joy and pleasure to him to be associated I with them and to be amongst such hearty and earnest I Christians. He knew that in them wr s the foundation of a good society, which would be stronger and stronger as the years went by, To all of them he tendered his very heartfelt thanks for the kind words which they had I said and which he did not think were altogether deserved —(1, Yes ")—in fact, he thought they had gone out of their own way to say some of the good, kind things which bad been said about him. It was to him a joy always to work amongst them and with them. There was not one of them who I would feel the severance of their connection mere than he would. Whilst all of them lost one member of the Guild be was losing them all, so comparatively his was the greater lose. He hoped that they might meet I again, if not in the immediate future he hoped in the far future where they would never part again. Be thanked them very much for the token. He would wear the badge and be proud of it, and would be ready to tell where it came from when asked. The birthday book was most valuable. When he saw the names written in it he would be able to see the fair faces in his memory. He valued it more for its associations than its intrinsic worth. He could say no more ; his heart was too full. The meeting was closed with prayer. The rev, gentleman afterwards conducted the evening service, and took an affecting leave of all the friends in Bold-street. At the open-air Mission, in Corporation- street, whioh has become so popular under his care. be I also gave a tarewell address. The congregations were especially large. AT BEWSEY-ROAD.

There was a large congregation on Sunday evening. at Bevisey-road Wesleyan elharcit, when the Rev C H Hocken preached his farewell sArmon. He based his discourse on C 'loss-ens 1 c,'.24, 27 and 28 ver. St Paul, he said, was pointing out the supremacy of Christ in all things ; in relation to God, in relation to this world and in relation to the church. Some people seemed to think that a minister's life was a very easy and desirable one. But did they think any tender-hearted man could go from house to house as a minister did, share the confid- ences of big people, and witness their physical weakness and anguish and suffe-ing, without becoming, a man of sorrewsland acquainted with grief ? " Then again troubles arose in the church, and there was, perhaps, a conflict of opinion. But the minister should be of les party ; he mast be a moderator ; exercise wise and generous impartiality, and strive to recognize the differ- ences existing among his people. The congregation did netlknow how such things worked upon 'the heart of a minister. He had never been so happy as when he bad been preaching Christ to them. Those had been times when he had felt more than ever the joy of his ministry. He went forth to his new sphere of labour with the determination to be more faithful to the church than , ever, and he was sure his joy would increase. lee had wished to get into more per3onal touch with them, se that he could more influence them for God. Of course he felt that men, and especially Lancashire men, were rather to be led than driven, but he would have been untrue to himself and unfaithful to his vocation, had he not sounded the note of alarm and warned every man against what was to come. What tact, sympathy, tenderness, insight, and knowledge a minister required in order to be at one with his people. He knew he had been a poor blunderer, and had fumbled about to find the door of their hearts. He had striven, as St Paul said, that he might present them all, perfect in Christ. To present them polished, refined, and moulded, so that they would meet with God's approval and acceptance, and that He would accept them as diadems in the Saviour's crown. For three years he had been journeying together with them. What had been the final outcome of it ? Had it been a period in which there had lo.en greater building going on in the church. The church was but a workshsp for the building of character. But it was character of a special type, character after the model and pattern of Christ Jesus. He would like to say how much he and his wife had felt their unvarying kindness towards them. He was bound to testify that they had always been most ready to follow any suggestion or Initiative of his, and always willing to carry on anything for the betterment of their church. He hoped they would enter into closer union with God, and give a greater share of their time to the interest of the church. The people of Bewsey-road were enshrined in the hearts of himself and wife and he would ask them to remember them in their prayers and they would journey on In different spheres but in the same direction and at last they would meet in heaven. During the service, Mr Rowland perfrarmed a violin solo and Mrs Arthur Parkinson Sang the solo part in the anthem " Angel Voices." The hymn " God be with you till we meet again " was sung at the evening ser- vice. Owing to the re-building of the organ, the ser- vices of an orchestral band were requisitioned, and they accompanied the singing. Mr W Brough conducted, and Mr B Wadsworth Presided at the piano. PRESENrATION TO MR. AND MRS. HOCKEN. Alderman Straw GREEN said the stewards and many conneetnd with that place of worship felt they could not let Mr. and Mrs. Hocken go from them without tender- ing to them some evidence of the love and esteem in which they are held. They would like to have done it at a week-night meeting, but that was not found to be convenient, and therefore they had taken advantage of the present opportunity. Mr Place had been indefatigable in getting up the pre- sentation. He had been most happily received in all quarters, and everyone had been most generous. Alder- man Shaw Green proceeded to read a letter from Mr J W Hayward,in which he said that the friends at Bewsey- road knew how much he prizsd and valued—hr was going to say—loved, Mr and Mrs Hocken. He wished they were able to still keep them amongst them, but Conference said " No." Their loss, however, would be the gain of the good people at Derby. In Mr Hocken they had had a friend, pastor, and faithful minister,who had laboured to give them his best. Mrs Hocken had been an ideal minister's wife, cheerfully and readily doing at all times her best, and coming amongst them to do anything she could to help on the good work at Bewsey-road. He (Alderman Green), eves sure that what Mr Hayward bad written was echoed by every one of them.

Mr POVEY was then called upon to make the PreEents" hon. Mr Hocken, he said, had served them faithfully and well for three yeare,and he was sure he was voicinK the feelings of the whole of the congregation, when be said they were grieved to part with him. They wished Mr and Mrs Hocken every happiness and comfort in their new sphere of labour, and trusted God's blessing would rest upon them. He believed Mr Hocken OA tried to live a life worthy of example. He had worked nobly and done his best to give satisfaction, and during the twa years he had occupied the position of steward, and had como into contac: with Mr Hocken he had met with nothing but courtesy and consideration from WM. For Mrs Hocken he could not find words to express the esteem in which she was held by the people of that church. When Mr Hocken came to them three years ago as 'pastor there were certain definite things theY expected of him, bat with Mrs Hocken it was quite different. They had no claim on her, but she had given her substance and time to a degree which they could not reasonably hive expected. He then presented to Mr Hocken a silver sacramental service, suitablY inscribed, and to Mrs Hocken a silver sugar basin and sifter, and expressed the hope that the recipients would spend many years of joy in their new sphere of labour. Mrs. HOCKENT, in acknowledging the gilt to herself, said she did net look so much at the gift as the love and affection which prompted it. They had won a warm place in her heart, and she would always remember them as friends with the kindest recollections. Mr. PiocxEm said he much appreciated the kindness which was behind the presentations to his wife and himself. It would serve as an inspiration to them when they went from that church to labour among new' friends, who did not know anything about them. They felt they had the confidence and love of those they had been with for three years, and he asked them to imagine what a comfort and help it would be to them in their future work. What had been said about them had, be thought, been prompted by genuine feeling, kindness and sympathy. He had learned something in Warring- ton, and it had been a happy place to live in. They would always speak well of tUe town. He would try to get into closer personal touch with the people and recog- nize the divine el ,ment in all men, lie felt greatly humbled by their sympathy, their affection, their gift, and wished he hid been able to do more for them. He trusted that the church would go forward and become a power in Warrington. He thanked them for the gift of a sacramental service which he would take with hint into the homes of the sick and the dying. They could not have given him anything which would touch him more deeply than that which spoke of the passion of our Lord and the sufficiency of His grace in the hour of suffering and death.

Alderman &Lew GREEN sail he was pleased to see Such a large cougrecation. Why were they not there regularly? The church was open, and the officialS looked for them, and he was sun they desired tke presence of everyone in the house of God.

CA.DISHEAD. On Sunday evening the Rev. Henry Scanes preached lais farewell sermon in the Wesleyan Chapel, Cadishead. There was a large congregation, and the choir sang "God be with you till we meet again," and the anthem "Now, Lord, we part." Mr E Hampson presided at the organ. The rev, gentleman leaves the Cadisbead circuit during this month for Tunstall.

Warrington Blue Coat School. The following report has been received by the Trustees from the Rev II I Wadeson with reference to his recent examination of the children:—Gentle- men,—l have the honour to lay b-fore you the re- port upon the above schools, examined this year on the 7th inst when 65 children were presented. M in previous years I desire again to record a higit general standard of efficiency, both in instructies and in oiscipline. Of the tiva roce subjects, Holt Scripture, English history and repetition are excel. lent. Grammar and geography good and reading very good. This applies to all standards. The paper work is uniformly neat and well arranged. ID the subject matter of the papers it is gratifying to note an advance in the composition exercises of the higher group,and in arithmetic notably in Standard VII. Singing and physical drill are also to be classed as excellent. The teaching of both subject 9 is evidently in most competent hands. Speaking of the results as a whole,l consider them to mark steady year's work conducted with ability and with success.

div.head: FUNERAL OF THE LATE CAPTAIN
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE LATE CAPTAIN
WILLIS.

The funeral of the late Captain H. R. d'A. Willis, Halsnead, near Prescot, took place at Whiston Church on Menchiv, ia the presence of a very large assembly of , local residents. Representatives of well-known famines were present. and the vllagers of the country side were there to show their affection for the squire who had proved himself a friend. A detachment of police under Inspector Crompton arranged the crowd,which included the children of the Whlston Schools, along the walks of the churchyard, and it was between the Brea of mourners that she procession, which bad been formed at the lych gate when the cortege drew up there,passed into the church. The service was choral. Mr Tusbing- barn, organist of the Prescot Paris's Chu, cis, presi3ed at the organ and played Beethoven's " Funeral March," " Blest ere the departed " (Spahr), and the " Funeral March " by Mendaleeohn before the arrival of the funeral party at the church. AS the procession—clergy. choir, coffin, end mournere—entered "Oh rest in the Lord" was played. The 90th Psalm was rendered to a chant, and after the lesson the hymn "On the Resurrection Morning " wag sung, while as the congre- gation filed out Chopin's "March Funehre" was played. The service in the church and at the graveside was taken part in by Bishop Royston, the Neve Canon Willis, rector of Warrington (brother ot the deceased), Canon Michell. of Presoot, and El 3 Wood, vicar of Whiston. At the side of the vault the burial sentences were ren- dered to froyte's chant, and before the Benediclion was proncmnced the choir sang the hymn" They whose course on earth is run." The coffin, which was covered with six wreaths, was borne into the vault by six men of the estate. The chief mourners were : Mr James Rinney (eon-in-law), Mrs G Vernon (d.aughPer)i Miss Willis and Miss G W Willis lstst:et9, Rev J and Mrs Brown (brother and sister-in- law). A Frodsham Farmer Heavily Fined.—Alleged
False Milk Warranty.

Before Messrs W S Barrett and E Cannizigton, at the bivernool County Magistrates' Court. on Tues- day, Thomas Ellams, farmer, Frodsham, was sum- moned for having given a false warranty in 1./thin n in respect of a quantity of milk he forwarded og the 24th Misy to the Garston agent (W H Abbott) of Messrs Warth and Co., known as the Callow Park Dairy Company. Mr Wilson, of the County Offices, Preston, prosecuted, and Mr F Turner, of Chester, defended. The case arose out of a prosecu- tion instituted by the police against Abbott, who upon the hearing of the summonses against him for selling milk to which ten per cent. of water had been added, satisfied the bench that be had sold the milk as be had received it from Ellams,and pro- doled Ellains's written warranty that the milk was pure. Owing to the bottle which contained the sample of the milk retained by the police having been broken,and the milk lost,Mr Turner submitted that its non-production was fatal to the prosecution against Ellams because the Act had not been complied with. The bench ruled against him on this point. At the timeEllams gave the warranty he bad reason to believe, Mr Turner said, that the statement it contained was quite true. Ellams now emphatically denied that any water had been added to the milk. The magis- trates stated that they considered the case proved. Mr Wilson informed the bench that Ellams had been twice previously convicted, once for extract- ing cream. The bench imposed a fine of .£2O and costs. Upon the applicatiou of Mr Turner a case , was stated.

div.head: lestters to the Ebitor. Municipal Bowling Green.
div.p: lestters to the Ebitor. Municipal Bowling Green.

'Dear Sir,---dt was I think gratifying to many to learn that the Council had received a proposal on this ques- tion in such a favourabla manner as they did at their last meeting. At no previous meeting has the question been so well received as it was at the last one. That I the making of bowling greens would be popular and of some benefit in the town I think few will venture to deny. No doubt a few persons object on the ground of expense, but I do not think these persons can have gone carefully into the matter. As a matter of fact bowling greens made in a public park or recreation grounds and managed in a systematic way entail very little e xpenee and the expense is so little, comparatively speaking,that it is scarcely felt on the rates of a town. See the reports on matters of this kind in other towns. I think the Corporation might at least venture at the present time to make two, say, vne in the Town Park, and the other inj Victoria Park, Latchford. At the same tirr e if they would erect a refreshment room in each of those 'places,where the bowlers and others could obtain a little refreshment, it would be a great boon. At present our parks are inadequately equipped in this respect. These rooms would help to popularise the parks a little more and tempt the mothers with the little ones to frequent the places a lit'ele more than they otherwise do.

May I also venture to say that if the Corporation would make these bowling greens it would be a wise policy on their part. It would at least demonstrate the thoughtful consideration of the pleasures of others. The present Corporation and the zeal and en!.erprizs it has shown during the past few years for the commercial and industrial welfare of the town deserves, I believe, the approbation of its ciitizens. May some ask that the same zeal and enterr, size be shown in the social wilfare of the town and tha the making of howling greens shall be an instalment in such social programme.—Youis truly,
E. ENGLAND.

div.head: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS
div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS
Cricket.

On Saturday the Widnes eleven visited Warrington for the second time this season and again sustained a severe defeat. The engagement was specially arranged to fill an open date on the Warrington fixture card, and several promising players in the second eleven were given the opportunity of displaying their abilities. The visitors made a very poor display at the wicket, being dismissed for the aggregate of 47. The Warrington bowlers did their work well, W Bennett capturing 3 wickets at a cost of 14 runs, whilst Lynes was respon- sible for 4 wickets at a cost of 4 runs 03- flampson took 2 wickets for 10 runs and D Plinston 1 for 3 runs. At the commencement of the match Lynes bowled Hampson in his first over, and directly after wards effected a fine catch in the slips which dismissed J Jones. A Gardiner (16) and J Parkinson (11) were the only Widnes batsmen to attain double figures.

The home team's innings was productive of 107 runs, B Silcock (34) being the chief contributor. B Thomp- son carried out his bat after compiling 29, and W Hind was responsible for 23. The result was particularly gratifying, when it was considered that the Warrington team was not a representative one, and the juniors are to be congratulated upon their performance.

Sankey Wire Mills entertained Platt Bridge 1.M., and the match ended in a draw, the odds being in favour of the Wire Mills, who were dismissed for 72. To this Platt Bridge had responded with 63 for the loss of 9 wickets when play ceased. Hughes (18), Clarke (17), and Taylor (16) batted in good style for the Wire Mills, and J Evans bowled effectively, capturing 5 wickets at a cost of 17 runs. J. Hewitt (20) and Jackson (19) were the top scorers for the vhiltors.

Fairclough's Mills met the League of the Cross, and gained the victory by a margin of 35. J Richardson was the top scorer for the winners,his *nnings realizing 13, whilst G Mather was responsible for 15 for the League of the Cross.

Messrs Peter Walker and Son's Warrington team met the eleven from Burton on Saturday, and the encounter resulted in a draw, each team compiling 45 runs. T Wright (16) and J Arber (11) were the chief contributors for Warrington.
Fairfield defeated Stretton and Appleton, the margin being 19. Barns and Boardman batted well, knocking up 13 and 11 respectively.

Latchford Baptists and Lowton met on the ground of the first named eleven, and the match ended in a draw slightly in favour of the visitors. Lowton went in first and compiled 88, the home team responding with 4.4 for eight wickets. Cliff (18 not out) was the top scorer for I the Baptists.

Cycling. At the Chorley Rural District Council meeting on Tuesday, the Surveyor (Mr Lawrence) astonished the members by stating that a bicycle caused more dust on the high roads than a hundred horse vehicles. The council, he said, might smile at the statement ; but from his observation he asserted that ninety per cent of the dust was owing to the fact that cycles sucked up the binding of the roads and dispersed it in clouds of dust. There is, doubtless, a modicum of truth in the statement, but if the Surveyor had blamed the motor car instead of the bicycle be would have been nearer the mark.
C. Berry, of Warrington, was third in the mile bicycle race at Congleton Corporation Sports on Saturday.
Rugby Football.

On the first page of this paper will be found an announcement of the Junior League which the senior club proposes to form. Applicatons have to be made to Mr. H. Ashton, who is in hopes that there may be sufficient entries to form a strong body of young players from the town and district.

On Tuesday night the playing members of Runcorn team had a practice, which, except for one unfortunate incident was of a most successful character. There were no fewer than 42 players on the field J Butter- worth, the centre three-quarter, twisted the knee which has given much trouble in the past, and he had to leave the field.

A Northern League meeting was held on Tuesday at Huddersfield when a number of clubs registered new players. Warrington put on their list the following local juniors : H S Bailey, S Warburton, J W Harmer A Brookes, J Webb, G Brade, J Burton, and N Coleman.

The footballers in this district will hear with regre of the shocking death of James Tanner the Hull three- quarter. He was a native of South Wales, formerly played for Mountain Ash and Penarth, and was killed at Barry on Wednesday. He went there in search of work and while stand near some trucks at the docks was crushed to death. It is only a short time since Tanner was a regular member of the Hull team—l believe he played occasionally last season, and most of the Northern League footballers knew him well.

That popular publication the "Athletic News "Foot- ball Annual has reached us. The interesting little book still published at the modest 3d., is as full as ever of useful information. Fixtures, club results, League tables, laws of the game, conference dates, particulars of international players, secretaries' addresses, and referees' list are all included within its yellow backs and in addition seven half•tone photos. of prominent players are included. It is published by E. Hutton and 1 Co., Ltd., at Withy Grove, Manchester, and 68, Fleet, street, London.

Good Templary at Warrington. The weekly seszion of the Temperance Mission Lodge of the lUG T was held in the Ebenezer Mission Room on Wednesday, Bro Merlin, C T presided over a good attendance. It was decided to re-open the Juvenile Temple next Wednesday. Sister Mrs Sheath was recommended as SJ T and Bro Griffiths as ABJ T. Two new members were initiated into the lodge. Bro Clarke, PD (Earlestown) gave an encouraging address. The programme for the evening was " Turn out the CT" and some amusement was caused by the questions that were asked by the members. In- structive questions were the chief points of the evening and a very enjoyable and profitable tithe was spent.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY AUGUST 22, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY AUGUST 22, 1902

with Tennyson been saying for over forty years, ' Behold, we know not anything: I can but trust that good shall fall At last far a, at last to all. And every winter change to spring, So runs my dream; but what am I ? An infant crying in the night; An infant crying for the light; And with no language but a cry." Dr trorton asks some pertinent questions of his Chris- tian readers. I have been asking the same for over forty years. " Will he excuse me because I speak about the salvation of the soul when I have neglected the obvious method of making these dear human bodies wholesome, these homes sw.et, these men courageous and happy, and these women secure from the degrada- tion of the street ?"

Some mouths ago Morgan came to San Francisco on a private train, each car being a sumptuous palace. He was accompanied by Bishop Potter, and other church dignitaries. During their visit they made arrangements foteperfectiug an association known as the " Civic Federation.' The object being to do away with strikes by'emeans of arbitration, or conciliation. I draw atten- tion to this because subsequent events have proved the folly of se-called Christians trying or pretending to try to settle labour questions, while they have under their very noses,and quite within their power to settle labour problems of such enormity as to appal all humanity. Those who have read Engel's "Condition of the , working classes in 1844," will be surprised to learn thee, the exact counterpart of those slavish conditions now I obtain in the southern states of this free and enlightened land. I could spsak of what! have seen, and Engel describes, of the horrors of the Lancashire cotton factor- ies fifty years agoond which horrors were only removed by the efforts of trade-unionists aided by the groat and good Lord Shattesburk: The American trade uuionist, has for years been spending money and labouring hard to put an end to child labdur in the American cotton ' factory, but when did a Morgan, or a Bishop Potter give either a cent or lend even a helping hand to civilize the factery owner, and yet they ere both millionaires a many times over. Heartless selfishness has joined hands with brutal ignorance, and we have child labour of so terrible a type that African slavery was heaven compared with it. "Boys and girls from the age of six years and upward are employed. They usually work from six o'clock in the morning until seven at night. For four months of the year, they go to work before daylight and they work until after dark. At noon these weazened pigmies topple over to sleep like a lot of babies. When it is time for work the foreman marches through the groups, shaking the sleepers, shouting in their ears, lifting them to their feet, and kicking them into wakefulness." A labour re- presentative travelled through the district and saw all this. He says, "I thought to lift one of the little toilers to ascertain his weight. Straightway through his thirty- five pounds of skin and bones there ran a tremor of fear, and he struggled forward to tie a broken thread. There were dozens of just such children in this mill. A physician who was with me said they would all be dead, probably in two years, and their places filled with others." There are five States that have no child labour restricting laws. The capital comes from the New England States. From a reliable source it is learned that a cotton mill having a pay-roll of six thousand dollars a week in New England, can be run in the Southern States for four thousand dollars a week. This means a saving of just one hundred thousand a year; and the mill having a capical of one million dollars thus gets a clear gain of ten per cent per annum. "These mills all have "Company Department Stores" where the employees trade. A certain credit is given, and the employee who has a dollar coming to him in cold cash is very, very rare.' The cashier of one mill said, " nineteen out of twenty families never see any cash, and probably never will.' Of the employing agent and his methods, and of the em- ployers control of the whole labour vote through debt I must pass over. capital is king and resides in Boston. Icstrad of :abolishing child labour, capital gives a lot near the mill property, to any preacher who will build a church. Within a quarter cf a mile of one cotton mill in South Carolina steed seven churches. The husband stays at home, and does house work, the wife and chil- dren being the factory workers, ten and fourteen cents per turn being the average for the children, slightly more for the mothers. A preacher speaking of the matter put it in this way. " Oh, of course, it is pretty bad—but then dear brother, you know the cuildren are better off in the mill than running the streets." In a further conversation with this same man of God he con- fessed without shame that many of the men whose whole families worked in the mills, subscribed one tenth of their income to the support of the Gospel and gave him an order on the mill company for the amount ; and this amount was withheld from wages and paid to him regu- larly by the cashier of the company. This is competition greed, and the trade unionist would, like an infant crying for the light, say, who will remedy this if I stand on one side. The average wage of the Pittsburgh miners is nine dollars and ninety cents per week. Think of it, and men and women positively rolling in such weath that it is beyond the powers of their own feeble minds to imagine ways and meane of spending it ! No labour leader that I am acquainted with,and I think I know most of them,cares one rap Fol Christianity and its preachers. If Christian men and women are seeking an opportunity to work for their Master, it is ready to their hands, SAVO His little ones! The labour unionist of the States is not wasting his time on Trusts. He knows they will prove a blessed object lesson only give them rope enouen.i

" I dwelt in a nation filled with pride; Her people were many, her lands were wide ; Her record in war and science and art Proved greatness of muscle and mini and heart. " What a grand old country it h I" I cried, And a man with his chest in the air replied, " It's Morgan's." • I went to heaven. The jasper walls Towered high and wide, and the golden halls Shone bright beyond. But a strange new mark Was over toe gate viz., " Private Park." And a saint with livery on replied Morgan's," I went to the only place left. "lii take A chance on the brimstone lake. Or perhaps I may be allowed to sit On the griddled floor of the bottomless pit." But a leering lout with horns on his face Cried out, as he forked me off the place " It's Morgan's." INTERESTING LOCAL WEDDING

div.head: PUT YOURSELF IN HIS PLACE.
div.p: PUT YOURSELF IN HIS PLACE.
Capital and Labour in America.
Startling Revelations.
[By Mr. H. Whitham.]

A rather long spell of sickness has prevented me from taking notice of quite a multitude of events that have engrossed, one might say, tha world's attention. The Boor war, and the peace, with its conditions. Our Western press teemed with its details, and thoughia few lamented the way of its ending, we distant sons and daughters rejoiced with you at home that the blunder- ing work was over. Again, the Coronation that was to be, with all its sad daily issue of bulletins that inevit- ably led up to the grievous disappointment of millions, and a postponement that meant great loss to thousands of tradesmen. The further issue of bulletins that spoke of hope that the royal patient might yet live to see the inside of the Abbey and come out a crowne l King. All these matters called for first attention as we took up our morning paper and conned its telegraphic news. I s ncerely hope ere this letter is read tha King will be all right, and will be crowned, and that all will be well in that direction.

It would take more time, and would lead me in a direction I wish to avoid to explain how it comes about that I, a republican, hold the views Ido at the present time touching royalty. All I may say now in explana- tion is, that few Englishmen could have gone through my past fourteen years experience without undergoing a similar mental change. For the present let it rest. My purpose in this letter is to deal with the hoary- headed-sinner known as the' labour question." I know not if my Warrington friends are kept as well posted in the affairs of the States, as we are with those of Great Britain. If they are, they know that in the labour world America never in its history knew such a state of unrest as it is now experiencing. This may seem strange when at the same time we have to acknowledge that business was never so good, workmen never before re- ceived such high wages, and never before were they in such demand. Fruit is actually rotting on the tress fcr want of help to gather it, Peaches, apricots and plums can be had almost for the asking. The California of to- day is not by any means the same as the California of ten years ago, and still strikes are the order of the day. A week's strike on the street railways resulted in its upwards of 2,000 men being paid at the rate of, one shilling per hour. Carpenters are getting 141 for ten hours, and freight handlers is per hour, with nearly double for over time.

Now where does the unrest come in ? In one of our morning papers appears an article on the extravagance in drees in which the writer Bays :—" In a time when any serious person must perceive the gravest possibili- ties of social change, and when the masses of the people are realizing to the full their political power, the chief instigator of social revolution, and the element much more dangerous to natienal peace than any petty group of anarchists,is the idle, insolently worldly class." Yes, the masses are realising their power. In several of our large c:ties they heaae elected working men as mayors San Francisco has as mayor one who played an instru- ment in one of our theatres, and he is giving the old politicians a few object lessons. But let us look at " the idle, insolent, worldly class." A New Ye rk bride was recently married in a gown that cost 10,000 dollars. Nearly all of the work was done by hand, and required almost the entire force for weeks of the establishment in which it was made. I suppose the writer of the editorial referred to would scarcely rank Mr Schwab among the idle class, though I should judge the " insolently worldly " would claim him. This man is President of the American Steel Trust, and receives the mere pittance of 1,000,000 dollars a year for his ser- vices. He has now given it out that he is about to build a house to live in. The interior decirations will be magnificent in the extreme. In the centre of the house will be a stair way of marble and onyx. The grand stairway, with its gorgeously coloured cathedral glass windows, mammoth pipe organ, galleries and columns reaching to the ceiling of the second floor, will cost half a million dollars. The whole to cost 2,500,000 dollars. The same Pittsburg paper that records this little matter of home bnileing informs us that " six deaths and a score of prostrations is the heat record for the past twenty-four hours. There was much suffer- ing among the mill-workers, and many were forced to return to their homes quite exhausted." The masses who are learning their power are noting these little matters, and they are closely watching Mr. Carnegie who is almost forced to confess his inability to glva away his millions, so fast does the gold roll in on him. The great masses of the people simply look upon the notorious chief of the homestead strike as giving away what does not belong to him. Now, by your leave, Mr. Editor, we will introduce our readers to a few of the ways in which the idle rich pass their time. An evening party was held recently for the purpose of christening some Maltese cats, this, in its turn was followed by a dinner given at Newport in honour of an African monkey. This is something more than silly, and even in its mei' foolishness we see to what depths society can descend, but let us look further. A writer in the New Yo k" Sun" speaking of a visit he paid to the Latin Quarter in Paris says During my my visit I talked with a couple of pretty girls,l one of whom I asked if she were dancing—you know they dance the can-can there with great expression— and she very naively told me she was not because she was not wearing socks that evening. "Socks ?" I queried, quite at a loss to understand. Oh yes," she explained, " you see when we dance the can-can we, 1 wear eocka. Show him, Marie," she aided, turning to her companion. And Marie showed me with the pretty and piquant delicacy of a Frenchwoman that her hose were what we usually call " half," but I am qnite sure they were not mere than an eighth, for they oid not get more than four inches above the shoe-tops. Later, when the fair maiden danced, I can readily understand why 1 the alleged half-hose made the can-can morel interesting than whole hose. Under these painful circumstances, I sincerely hope that the sock I is not general among the ladies of the Quaker City.—A 'further search brought out the following interesting information touching women's gear, and the way in which the profits of labour are spent, and now the initial scenes are laid in England. The swagger set having introduced the' sock,' now seek to inteeduce the sandal. All they ask is " Are they artistic ?" " Are they becoming F' "Are they fashionable?" If the last question is answered in the affirmative the rest goes. When an English beauty and fashion leader lifted her fluffy petticoats a little higher than is usual in her friend's boudoir the girls nearly tumbled out of their chairs. There was no denying it They actually saw socks. What lam writing I know to be true, and any American dry goods store window offoam proof. OF course the windows only are my proof. Leaving the socks ard still attending to the shop windows, we see stockings with all the monograms, and forget-me-note the artist could think of worked up the front. If the foundation is silk a more fetching hose cannot be imagined. Of course these are to be worn with low boots or slippers, else what avail would this work be ? Hand painted hose takes the first place on the flivoloue list. The questionennw in order is, what do they cast ? Not much only from 100 do! to 300 dol a pair,and even sometimes mere when they are painted by a fine artist and interwoven with jewels. Heavily incrusted bead hose are not so costly. These may be had at from 20 dots to 60 dole. Enough of the hose side of extrava- gance ! Lady riegernon Lennox recently came oat here accom- panied by her husband. Their purpose was to hunt mountain lions and bears. A couple of columns sufficed to describe her wardrobe. Among these I find: " entire costume of poulain, which in plain English means colt., Both skirt and coat were made of the glossy, downy coat of a new born horse and stitched and trimmed wiLlo bands of cloth of the same shade. Recentle a New York jeweller had an order for a complete set of trousers buttons, to be made of gold and ornamented with opals and enamel. Even bracelets for men are becoming fashionable and young swells wear a gold snake,modeled after an Egyptian antique around their upper arms A jeweller who was interviewed on this matter raid,—l hear that thin gold collarettes are now faehionable the sort of things that in early times used to he called eorgets. Some of them are made of thin plates of gold while others are made of chain-work, like the old- fashioned chain mail. Armlets for men are made in several patterns, some being merely large haneles,while others clan, on the upper arm and are locked in place by a email gold pad lock, similar arrangements are also made for the thighs and ankles. One may well ask, where is it to end ? It can only end when we cease to pay a corporation Is sever a 500,000 dot fee, and a cor- poration President 1,000,000 dols. a year. Even in the columns of your own " Examiner "it is easy to note the march of extravagance. As the swell weddings march by we see bow the wedding presents increase in number and value. The social tax must soon become so' oppressive that some one must before long call a halt. Lady Helen Stewart of the Leon- 1 donderry family had recently a phenomenal recorel.Thiel lady received 728 presents, the estimated aggregate of i which is 750,000 dollars. In New York recently Mr Whitney. spent 25,000 dollars to introdsce his step- daughter to New York's four hundred. I' can fancy the reader saying,—" hold, enough, it is growing mono- townie." It is my friend, and the position of a vast numb.' of working slaves has been so from the year one. Do you weary of the tale of worthlese idleness on the Part of the werlds Morganizerse then let us turn tn_tbe wealth creators.

Having read this, turn to the "Chrietian World " wherc a antics of articles will he fonnd touching "Town Problems " written by G H Garcia. These matters 'tight not to be monotonous to any one ealling himself human. I am ratting fairly well Et ricken in years, nearing the goal in fact. I have

div.head: Williamson—Deyes.
div.p: Williamson—Deyes.

On Wedsesday afternoon one of the prettiest and most fashionable weddings of the season was solemnized at the •;Victoria Park, Wesleyan Church, Wsvertree. The contracting parties were Mr Edgar Bertram Deyen, of wavertree, youngest son of Mr W Deyes, accountant, Liverpool, and MiFs Winifred (Winnie) Hannah William- son, fourth daughter of Mr Joseph Williamson, head chemist at Messrs Gossage and CO's, Widnee. The bride and bridegrooth are exceedingly well known throughout the whole of a very large district and consi.lerable interest was manifested in the ceremony. Mr Des 03, who holds a responsible position in the head office of the 'limited Alkali Cr., Limited, is one of the most popular organists who ever presided at Lodge-lane Wesleyan Church, while the bride's parents were, to a short time *go, closely identified with the Wesleyans in Hale Bank and Widnes. Not only was the bride for a long time s I prominent member of the choir at Hale 'Bank Wesleyan Church, but she rho took a warm interest in Sunday school work which she still maintained ors her removal to Wavertree. Mr. Williamson, the feaber of the bride, is one of the foremost gentlemen in Widnes—a fact which lends additional interest to the happy occasion under notice.— Long before the time announced for the arrival of the bride and her suite the church was filled with a fashion- able congregation who took their seats to the tuneful strains of a bridal intermezzo played by Mr Herbert , Jones, organist. Sbcrtly before two the bridegroom took up his position at the communion rail together with his best man Mr Spencer Bowler of Southport. A few minutes later the bride, leaning on the arm of her father, arrived and joined the wedding party waiting to receive her. Attired in a dress of white Indian silk, trimmed with antique lace, and wearing a Court train trimmed with orange sprays and chiffon, surmounted by a coronet of orange blossom with silk embroidered veil, the bride looked very beauti- ful. She aI9O wore a handsome diamond ring, the gift of the bridegroom, and carried a magnificent shower bouquet composed of white lilies, white dahlias, and maiden-hair fern. The bridesmaids were Miss Maggie Williamena (sister of the bride), and Miss Florrie , Knowles, Runcorn (niece). The former was attired in a a lovely dress of pink Bengaline silk, trimmed I with white silk embroidery, with a picture hat trimmed with white chiffon and white poppies. Miss Knowles was attired in a lovely dress of white Indian silk trimmed with Valenciennes lace and insertion with hat to match. Both bridesmaids carried beautiful shower bouquets cemposel of white asters, white dahlias, white lilies, sprayed with mai-len hair fern and wore gold bangles, the gift of the bridegroom. The marriage ser- vice, which was most impressively conducted by the Rev John Bramh,aeeisted by the Rev Samuel Affarrinttovas concluded with the singing of "The Voice that breathed o'er irAden." The bride was given away by bar father, and the departure of the wedding party took place to the noble chords of Wagner's Bridal March from " Lo- hengrin." A reception WAR afterwards held at "Penrhos," the residence of the bride's father, which was attended by upwards of ISO guests. Subseqnently the harms' pats left for Norl'h WsIPS, where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's travelling dress was a fawn costume with hat to match. The newly-married pair were the recipients of about one hundred presents of a valuable character.

LO.G.T. HOPE OF EARLESTOWN LODGE.

The above order held their usual weekly meeting on Monday night in the Co-operative Hall Barles- town. The quarterly reports were read and shewed a balance of 178 40 in hand in the Adult Lodge and 198 9il in the Juvenile Lodge. Interesting readings were given by Bro. Newman, Woods and J Wilson and songs were rendered by Bro Hatton and Sister Owens. AICUORQUODALR AND Cos. EXCURSIONS.

The annual excursion for the workpeople of Messrs McCorquodale and Co , of Newton, taok place on Saturday, the destination this year, as it has been for several years past, being Liverpool and Blackpool. The day was gloriously fine, and con- sequently a very large number of people took the opportunity of having a visit to the seaside. An equally large number journeyed to Liverpool and thence to New Brighton, and in each case a thoroughly enjoyable day was spent. The arrange- ments were in the hands of the officials of Messrs McCorquodale, and they were efficiently carried out.

div.head: CORONATION PICNIC AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: CORONATION PICNIC AT EARLESTOWN.

Following on the heels of the Barlestown Co- operative Society, Mr Thomas Molyneux of Market- street gave to his customers, what he termed a Coronation picnic;' on Saturday afternoon. Strik- ing out on novel lines, Mr Molyneux engaged the Mission Hall in which to supply the tea and refreshments, and a field belonging to Mr. Mort, farmer, in which the guests could disport themselves. He engaged a host of workers, and how necel.sary it was that a very large number should be employed, will be gathered from the fact that nearly 4,000 adults and juveniles were regaled with refresh- ments at seven sittings. This host assembled on the field at half-past one, and led off by the Viaduct Prize Band, the vast assemblage sang the hymn " All people that on earth do dwell," and afterwards the " Coronation Hymn." Sports were then pro- ceeded with until 4 o'clock, consisting of fiat races, boot-lacing race, potato gathering race for I boys and girls. Tea was then served out at the Mission Hall, and this was no light task to those engaged. However, everybody was finally satisfied. Other contests such as egg and spoon races, sack races, tug of war,sewing lon buttons, illustrations by women how to save life in case of fire, and how to rescue a child from drowning, the Viaduct band at intervals rendering selections of music. This brought the proceedings Ito 715 p.m. Shortly afterwards the hymn "God ' be with you till we meet again," was sung and the proceedings were brought to a conclusion by the singing of the National Anthem. The novelty of the affair appealed to the people, and they thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

div.head: SINGULAR CASE AT WARRINGTON. Revelations at – the County Court. Allegations Against Trustees.
div.p: SINGULAR CASE AT WARRINGTON. Revelations at - the County Court. Allegations Ag- ainst Trustees.

Ur Crompton (Messrs Browne and Cr)mpton) made some singular revelations at the Warrington County ICourt on Thursday, which led his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands to remark that if the fasts were as stated , they constituted a gross fraud. The allegations wore made during the hearing of a Case in which Mr Marks representing Mr Wolfe Jacksoo,manee-19nder of Chester sought to obtain a judgment for £l5 33 6d against Philip Robinson, a porter in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee at Warrington Central 'Station, and Frederick Robinson, a news agent of Orford-lane. Mr. Crompton, said he was not appearing profession- ally in the case, but wished to say on behalf of the defendants that some time ago judgment was obtained ! against them for the ruin of £lO. That judgment was gazetted in the usual way and shortly afterwards a Birmingham firm sent a circular letter to the defendants ! saying that as they yew in monetary difficulties they were willing to assist them. A representative came to Warrington and told defendants that if they would sign a paper everything would be all right. He got defend- ants to execute a document, which afterwards was discovered to be a deed of assignment of all their pro- perty for the benefit of their creditors. The trustee then said he would not realize their estate, provided they would pay 12s a weak for the purpose of purchas- ing the estate back from the trustee. The amount so realized was afterwards to be distributed among the creditors who assented. The sum of £l6 was paid at the rate of 129 a week,and then defendants began to fall into arrear. An auctioneer wassent down from Birming- ham, who said be was authorized by the trustee to sell, and he did so, His (Mr Crompton's) firm had Written several letters to the firm in Birmingham. but had been unable to get any satisfactory information regarding the matter. With respect to the present claim the defend- ants did not dispute it. Tney borrowsd 11 103 In the first instance and had repaid £8 17s 6J. The claim of £l5 33 61 was for interest and balance due. The wife ef Phillip Robinson was called, and said Ms Crompton's statement was quite true. His Honour remarked that these was no blame attached to Mr Jackson, and continued : That is the way of assisting people out of debt, is it ? Did they advance you any money ? Mrs Robinson . No your houour. We never had a penny from them. Mr Msrks said they knew nothing of the deed of assignment. Mrs Robinson : The representative who came from Birmingham took a list of auditors and said they would write to them. Mr Marks We have never heard from them. His Honour (to Mrs Robinson) : I hope you won't sign anything again without asking somebody's advice about it. That is a curious way of assisting creditors. It is a very shocking thing. The greatest publicity should be given to such cases.
. Ms Honour (to Mr Marks) : I will ask you to with- draw the summons. I cannot make a commitment. Mr Crompton : I will give Mr Marks the name of the tragtee:

• His Honr,ur (to Mr Marks) : I hope you will make inquiry. Upon he facts as seated it is a gross fraud. It is sometimes very difficult to dual with these people. Sometimes there is no firm or fixed place of businesu. I don't know whether it is so in this case.

Mr Crompton : riar-eir—r-ePTieTt.o-O"ni-letters haVe not been satisfactory-. Mg Honour : It 1.F7 a case that demands the fullest investigation. If this sort of thing exists no judge will make a commitment against the defendan,. /am glad it has been brought before the Court. Mr Uneworth (solicitor) pointed out that it N 9451 open to any creditor to take action against the trustee for an account. Mr Crlinpton : We have not haen able to get bold of a creditor.
His Honour (to Mr 'Marks) This is well worth your while considering bcause con will not be able to get a commitment in cases; where this has taken piace. _ . .
The case was withrirawa, Mr Marks sating that he would maim inquiries.

div.head: Unfounded Allegation against a Brother.
div.p: Unfounded Allegation against a Brother.
Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at St. Helens ' Town Hall. on Monday,on William Catheart,aged twenty-five, of 56, Island's-brow, who died on Friday evening from a pistol

The Coroner, said the police reported to him that deceased shot himself in 'a field near his nome after giving his brother John a note to take to his mother, in which be said he was going to destroy himself. Some persons had since set out a report that John had shot deceased, bat the police inquired into the matter, and there appeared nothing in it. If the inquest was ad- journed until Thursday probably they would find that nineteen or twenty people shot him: Mrs Cathcart said her son was twenty-five years of age. He had been in South Africa with the 3rd (Militia) Battalion South Lancashire Regiment. Since be returned from the front, about nine months ago, deceased had done very little work, and had been drink- ing heavily. On Friday he appeared so strange that ells was frightened. John Cathcart, the brother, saLl he beard a shot, and went to deceased in a wood, about 300 yards away. Deceased gave him a note and some powder, shot, and caps, and witness went borne with them.
-The Coroner : What did you leave your brother by himself with the pistol for ? Why didn't you wallop him and take the pistol from him ? Witness ; I was not going to try ; be might have done me.

The Coroner : He bad fired the pistol off. You ought to have hit him under the ja w,tied him up with a rope, and put him under restraint. It would have done him good. Witness : He said, " Will thou go back I' " and I said " No," and he said, "I will do thee,if thou doesn't." I turned to go, but before I had gone two strides I heard the shot and saw him fall.

Constable Heaton spoke to the death. Cathcart had put the pistol in his mouth, and the charge bad gone out of the right side of his head. Witness had bad com- plaints of deceased carrying the pistol, and on one occasion stcpped and searched him for it. He had threatened to shoot people. Clara Ashbrook,aged twelve, of 50, Islapd's-brow,said she heard deceased talking to his brother John,and then saw bim take the pistol from his pocket and shoot him- self. John did not do it. The Coroner said John need not be alarmed at what people said. It was clear he did not do it. The jury returned a verdict of 'Suicide while insane."

div.head: LARGEST VESSEL IN THE WORLD.
div.p: THE LARGEST VESSEL IN THE WORLD.
Launch of the Cedric.

There was launched on Thursday last from the yard of Messrs Harland and Wolff, Limit Pd. Belfast, the twin-screw steamer "Cedric " of 21,000 tons gross register, Hitherto the "Celtic," belonging to the Oceania Steam Navigation Company, Limited (White Star Line), has for ever twelve months held the palm as the largest steamer afloat, but she is now displaced from this proud position by the " Cedric," which, although practically a replica of tier elder sister,is of slightly greater tonnage by reason of some small differences in details of con- struction.

The " Cedric "is intended for the Company's Pas- senger Service between Liverpool and New York, and may be expected to take her place on the berth in November next, running in conjunction with the " Cymric! " and " Celtic," which vessels have deservedly gained great popularity in the New York trade. This very important addition to the fleet of the White Star Line will materially assist in attracting via Liver- pool the great stream of travel to and from the United States with which the port is SD closely identified,and if, as is confidently anticipated, the same measure of suc- cess in wideaing the esteem of the travelling public be achieved by the " Cedric," as has been gained by the other steamers of the Lime, the enterprise of the Com- pany in adding another monster vessel to those already hanine. from the Port of Liverpool will be amply re- warded.

Warrington School of Art Technical Scholarships. The following are the rules relating to the new class of Middleton scholarships which is offered for the first time this year :—A technical scholarship shall be of the value of £5, for one year, together with evening class fees at the Warrington School of Art, in addition. Scholars shall be boys who have been in reguhr attendance at an elementary school in Warrington for not less than two years, and are actually engaged in trades requiring artistic skill. Candidates must have passed one at least of the art examinations of the Board of education, and must submit to a further test examination if required. Scholars may be re-appointed, at the discretion of the trustees, for a secund and a third year. Scholars shall attend three evenings weekly at the School of At, following such a course of study as the head- master may direct.

Deserter Breaks out of Warrington Barracks. At the Liverpool City Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr Stewart, a youth named Malcolm Healey, 17 years of age, was charged with stealing the sum of £2 9s 61, the money of David Edwards, a van- man employed by the Liverpool Parcels Delivery Company, who resided in ' Gloucester-street. At three o'clock that morning,whi/st in bed,prosecutor heard a noise in the room, and saw the prisoner on his hands and knees. Edwards caught hold of him and recognized him as having been employed as vanman by the Parcels Company. Prosecutor found his money on prisoner, who had entered the house by means of a window. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sent to gaol for three months. Healey was also committed on a charge of being a deserter from the King's (Liverpool) Regiment. The record- clerk(Sergeant Evans)said prisoner was committed only last month for being a deserter from the same regiment, and had afterwards broken out of Orford Barracks, Warrington.

The Crops. The fine weather of Saturday enabled the farmers to make a start among the oats, which, due to the large quantity of rain this season, are in a rough state, and will require carefui cutting. Wheat, of which there is more than in other years, is excep- tionally good, the straw long and the ears full. At present the wheat is standing very well, and only requires more sunshine to bring it to full perfec- tion. There is every prospect of a good second crop of clover, and potatoes are turning out fairly well. Cabbages are in tine condition, and it is expected that celery will also do well. 411, Dr Parker who is staying in BuckinghaFnshire is pro- gressing favourably towards coavalescence. Be hopes to take the Thursday service at the City Temple on the last Thursday in September.

THE DEATH AND GRAVE OF MOSES Through dreary wastes and gorges wild The ransomed tribes their way pursued; By doubts and fears at times beguiled, Though still sustained by angels' food. At last in Jordan's vale they rest Far from the desert's toils and cares ; And see the land of Canaan blest, So soon to be for ever their.. But where is now their faithful guide, Their leader all the journey through ; Whose gentle soul they olt,n tried By murm'rings and rebellion too ? Far up on Nebo's summit lone The prophet stood with beaming eye; Hi el time had come, his work was done, And thither he had gone to die. The dreary wilderness was past, The forty years of warerring o'er ; And grateful, he beheld at last The promised land from shore to shore. And truly, as the Lord bad said, It was a land of brooks and rills : Of oil and wine, and milk and bread, Imbosomed in eternal kills. But Moses' feet might never pace Those shining hills and valleys : For he, of all the chosen race' Had then on lot or portion there, He mu:maned not ; 'twas God's decree, And all His ways were surely just • Though dark the providence might be, Still in Jehovah was his trust. Than as the evening shadows stole All sot tly o'er the land and deep; A holy rapture filled his seal, And charmed that weary soul to sleep. No mortal saw that death serene, No mourners there a vigil kept ; But far away beyond the scene, The host of God in sorrow wept. A lonely grave in Moab's land, Where purple bills makstic rise ; The Prophet's God for him had plann'd, And fenced it in from human eyes. That grave by angels hands was made, And angels bore him from the hill ; To rest Within its sacred shade, Those angels for its guardians still, The will birds know the Prophet's grave, The lasting hills surround the spot, And desert fl)wers upon it wave ; But where—alas, man knoweth not J.
